sections.title: Abstract
sections.content: Beam is a sparse Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) model with 501.3B total parameters and 23.4B active parameters, specifically built and optimized for coding, reasoning, and agentic workloads. Beam delivers frontier level reasoning, while requiring 3-4x less inference compute than many models of its class. Pretrained on 23.8T diverse, curated, high-quality tokens, Beam features a 1M-token context window achieved through a novel two-stage midtraining phase, built on verifiable, correctness-anchored data. Post-training leveraged a large-scale, fully asynchronous reinforcement learning (RL) campaign across 10.5K GB300 GPUs, generating over 100M rollouts over 4 weeks of training. We believe this is one of the largest scale RL runs conducted by any open lab to date. Across our evaluation suite, capabilities continued to improve as we increased RL compute, with no sign of a plateau. Supported by deep hardware-model co-design, FP8/NVFP4 quantization, and a 1.93B-parameter speculative decoding drafter (DFlash 2), Beam maximizes serving throughput with efficient, flexible deployment. Averaged across conversation turns and harm categories, Beam refuses or pivots on 88.9% of harmful requests while complying with 81.5% of harmless requests, achieving the highest refusal/pivot rate on harmful requests among open-weight models on the Pareto frontier.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content: We are introducing Beam, Reflections first open-weight model. Beam is sparse Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) model with 501.3B total parameters and 23.4B active parameters across 52 layers, 256 experts, and 152K vocabulary size, specifically built and optimized for coding, reasoning, and agentic workloads. Beams capabilities stem from major investments across pretraining, midtraining, post-training, and infrastructure. Beam advances the Western open-weight frontier and achieves competitive performance with larger models like GLM-5.2 while approaching Qwen 3.8-Max on LongBench-v2, while delivering frontier-level reasoning, while requiring 3-4x less inference compute than many models of its class. The foundation of Beams efficiency and numerical stability lies in rigorous data curation and controlled scaling. Pretrained on 23.8T diverse, curated, high-quality tokensincluding high-value STEM, math, and code tokens preserved via novel domain-specific curation pipelines and internet-scale OCRBeams scaling held predictably across four orders of magnitude in pretraining compute, training models from 300M to 23.4B active parameters. Beams base architecture employs auxiliary-loss-free load balancing with cosine decay, sequence-level balancing, and depth-based residual scaling to achieve near-uniform expert utilization and bounded residual norms. It was pretrained end-to-end in under four weeks on 6,144 NVIDIA GB300 GPUs with 92.3% goodput toward the end and 21% MFU during steady-state training, after accounting for restarts. To bridge foundational knowledge and agentic execution, novel two-stage midtraining pipeline expanded Beams effective context length to 1M tokens on correctness-anchored data without degrading general capabilities. Posttraining was centered around high-compute reinforcement learning (RL) campaign, where our high-compute RL run generated over 100M rollouts on 10.5K NVIDIA GB300 GPUs over four weeks of training. We believe this is one of the largest scale RL runs conducted by any open lab to date, enabled by fully asynchronous platform with 110K concurrent rollouts, fast 12-second weight updates, and 99.99% dynamic batch packing, Beam organically developed tool-use, web browsing, and problem-decomposition capabilities. Across our evaluation suite, capabilities continued to improve as we increased RL compute, with no sign of plateau. For serving, Beam leverages hardware-model co-design, FP8/NVFP4 quantization, and DFlash 2 (a 1.93B-parameter speculative decoding drafter) to reduce memory footprint and maximize throughput. Safety and alignment were prioritized across the entire model development cycle. Pretraining filtered harmful content and PII, while post-training combined deliberative alignment SFT with context-aware RL across multiturn, jailbreak, and agentic tasks. Dedicated safety and RL teacher capabilities were merged using multi-teacher on-policy distillation (MOPD). Under Reflections Open Safety Framework (OSF), we assessed Beam as Limited across all four systemic-risk categories: Biological Weapons, Chemical Weapons, Loss of Control, and Cyber Offense. Limited rating means there is no material shift in the offense-defense balance attributable to the model and no material expansion of the threat landscape relative to comparable open-weight models. These findings are complemented by external third-party assurance evaluations. In the Iris Safety Evaluations (ISE) benchmarks we developed in-house to span single-turn, multi-turn, jailbreak, and agentic evaluations, Beam achieves an 88.9% refusal/pivot rate on harmful requests while complying with 81.5% of harmless requests. Scaling the alignment teacher from 100B to 501B parameters cut false-positive over-refusals by 48.7%, proving greater model capacity can substantially improve responses to permissible requests under the same safety-training setup. Beam Model Technical Report, Reflection Team et al.

sections.title: 2 Pretraining
sections.content: 2.1 Recipe 2.1.1 Model Architecture Beam is decoder-only sparse Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) Transformer [1, 2], designed for efficient long-horizon agentic reasoning. Beam leverages SandwichNorm [35], Group Query Attention (GQA) [6] with QK normalization [7], interleaved local and global attention [4, 8], Rotary Embeddings [9], SwiGLU [10] experts, and DeepSeek MoE-style [11] auxiliary-loss-free load balancing. We used RMSNorm [12] for all normalization layers, and used untied input/output embeddings. We applied soft capping to cap the final output logits at 30 [13]. Table 1 lists Beams configuration and hyperparameters. We elaborate on individual components of our architecture below. Configuration Beam Number of Layers Total Parameters Activated Parameters Hidden Dimension MoE Hidden Dimension Total Experts per Layer Activated Experts per Token Number of MoE Layers MLP Hidden Dimension Number of Dense Layers MLP/MoE Activation Function Query Heads KV Heads Head Dimension Attention Mechanism Attention Normalization Sliding Window Size Positional Encoding Embedding Vocabulary Size 52 501.3B 23.4B 5120 2560 256 8 49 20480 3 SwiGLU 48 8 128 Mix of local and global (5:1) QKNorm + Gated Attention 512 Local attention: RoPE Global attention: NoPE Untied 151936 Table 1: Beam configuration and hyperparameters. Attention We adopted an interleaved local-global attention pattern [4] with local-to-global ratio of 5:1; local attention layers use sliding window size of 512 tokens. To further reduce the KV-cache footprint, we employed GQA, coupling 48 query heads with 8 key-value heads at head dimension of 128 [6]. We use RoPE [9] with base frequency of 10,000 in local attention layers, and NoPE [14] in global attention layers. To improve attention stability, we leveraged QK normalization [7]. While removing the learnable gain parameters from QK normalizations RMSNorms strictly bounds the attention logits, we observe that doing so degrades long-context extrapolation, and so we retain them. We observed the model was susceptible to significant activation outliers after the attention output projection even when using QK normalization, so we adopted elementwise gated attention [15]. We compute gate vector 𝐠ℎ for each attention head ℎ as: 𝐠ℎ = 𝜎(𝐆ℎ𝐱 + 𝐛ℎ), where 𝐱 ℝ𝑑 is the RMSNormed input to the self-attention sublayer, 𝐆ℎ ℝ𝑑ℎ𝑑, 𝐛ℎ ℝ𝑑ℎ are trainable parameters, and 𝑑 and 𝑑ℎ are model and head dimension, respectively. We effectively suppress the attention stream by initializing the bias vector to -2.5 and initializing the gating matrices to be very small. Our preliminary experiments with headwise gated attention [16] and attention sinks [17] were less effective in either reducing gradient spikes or in promoting long-context modeling. (2.1) 6 Beam Model Technical Report, Reflection Team et al. To improve length extrapolation, we followed the scalable softmax approach of Nakanishi [18], which scales the attention logits of each query based on its absolute position. To improve stability, we used the following root-compression formulation to scale logits: (1 + 0.1 , 𝑝 2048 ) (2.2) where 𝑝 is the position index, rather than the formulation used by Nakanishi [18]. Mixture of Experts Our MoE architecture largely follows that of DeepSeek-AI et al. [11], with the exception that we did not use shared experts. We leveraged top-k router with sigmoid gating. Expert biases were added to the router logits for top-k selection. The router probability is computed from the unbiased logits. We normalized routing scores before combining the expert outputs. To ensure balanced expert utilization, we adopt the auxiliary-loss-free load balancing method of Wang et al. [19] with additional sequence auxiliary loss. To improve expert balance even when exposing the model to datasets not drawn from the pretraining data distribution, we used relatively high sequence auxiliary loss coefficient of 5 104. To avoid router logit saturation, we added router z-loss term with coefficient of 105. We used an expert bias update rate of 103. Despite the above mechanisms, MoE routing can become unstable at large scale, particularly later in training. We opined that it is detrimental to use constant learning rate to update the expert bias once the routing distribution has largely converged, when learning may be more sensitive to routing outliers. With that, we replaced the constant expert bias update with an adaptive update schedule: 𝜂bias(𝑡) = 1 2 𝜂max bias [1 + cos (𝜋 max (0, 𝑡 𝑇𝑤 𝑇 𝑇𝑤 ))] (2.3) is the maximum learning rate ( 103 in our case), 𝑇 and 𝑇𝑤 are the total training and warm-up steps, where 𝜂max bias respectively. The above scheme uses constant expert bias update during the warm-up period to ensure early routing convergence. Then it follows that the cosine learning rate decays to 0. This simple change significantly improves routing stability, and generalizes to models at Beams scale. Residual Stability At large scale, the residual stream can suffer from unbounded magnitude growth and activation outliers. Below we describe several interventions to prevent blowup. We note that we computed the entire residual stream in FP32, by upcasting sublayer outputs before adding them. To keep activations within reasonable range, we apply SandwichNorm to all sublayers [35, 20]; SandwichNorm normalizes both the input to and output from each sub-layer. In this way, the residual activations are decoupled from the internal dynamics of each sub-layer and largely depend on SandwichNorms output normalization. We initialize SandwichNorms output gains to 1 , where 𝐿 is the total number of layers [21], and input gains to 1.0, 𝐿 which we found to be the most empirically effective. Depth-Scaled Residual Connection. In pre-normalization architectures, including SandwichNorm, the residual stream 𝐱𝑛 is effectively direct summation of all preceding sublayer outputs 𝐡𝑡 (e.g., attention, MLP, 𝑡=1 𝐡𝑡, and so the activation magnitude inevitably increases with network depth. The curve shows the busiest experts load divided by the uniform-routing load, averaged across MoE layers; the dashed line marks perfect balance. The ratio reaches 1.04 at pretraining completion. Note that the index 𝑛 indexes sub-layers (e.g., attention, MoE) rather than full transformer layers. Empirically, we observe that the activation norm in early layers can be quite small due to the depth-scaled gain initialization in SandwichNorm, but that this does not interfere with learning. 2.1.2 Training Recipe Initialization Specific initialization schemes for the gains in the output RMSNorms of SandwichNorm and for gated attention parameters were described above. Linear layers were initialized with standard fan-in initialization, RMSNorm gains were initialized with 1s, and input embeddings were initialized from normal distribution with standard deviation equal to 1 𝑑, where 𝑑 is the hidden dimension. Hyperparameters and Optimization For optimization we used the AdamC algorithm [22] and linear warm-up plus cosine decay learning rate schedule, for more details see Appendix B. We use decoupled weight decay [23], with the weight decay term following the squared warm-up and cosine decay schedule reaching zero at the end of training. We apply weight decay to all parameters except biases and RMSNorm gains. The AdamC weight decay schedule correction is used for all regularized parameters, not only for parameters followed by normalization layers. Beam Model Technical Report, Reflection Team et al. Figure 2: Beam training loss in bits per byte (logarithmic scale) over the course of its pretraining run. Table 2 summarizes the optimizer hyperparameters used for the final pretraining run. We set up scaling ladder [24] where every tier is trained at constant number of tokens per (active) parameter (TPP) for any ablation. We maintain constant aspect ratio (width-todepth) throughout the ladder. The ladder tiers contain model configurations ranging from approximately 300M to 6B before the target tier of 23B active parameters. In practice, we have found little signal in configurations with fewer than 0.5B active parameters. After fitting FLOPs-to-validation-loss scaling law to baseline models performance at each tier, we can determine whether an intervention has increased compute efficiency by calculating the number of FLOPs necessary to attain the interventions loss under the baseline scaling law [24]. We accept the intervention if it reliably increases compute efficiency across tiers (i.e., it results in validation losses that would require significantly more FLOPs under the baseline scaling law), and does not hurt model stability or downstream evaluations. Compute efficiency (CE) is the ratio between the compute the baseline would require to achieve the interventions validation loss and the compute used by the intervention. For each validation dataset, we fit power law to the 9 Beam Model Technical Report, Reflection Team et al. baseline ladder, 𝐿base(𝐶) = 𝑎𝐶𝑏 + 𝑐, where 𝐶 is training compute in FLOPs, 𝑎 > 0 is the scaling coefficient, 𝑏 < 0 is the scaling exponent, and 𝑐 is the fitted asymptotic loss. For an intervention achieving loss 𝐿 > 𝑐 with compute 𝐶, its compute efficiency is: CE(𝐶, 𝐿) = 𝐿1 base(𝐿) 𝐶 = 1 𝐶 ( 𝐿 𝑐 𝑎 ) 1𝑏 . (2.6) Where 𝐶𝐸 > 1 indicates an improvement over the fitted baseline. In practice, we found that statistically significant change in either direction must register CE change above 5% to cancel training-seed noise and sampling noise. Crucially, every pretraining recipe intervention must be ablated on the scaling ladder to measure its compute efficiency trend. We applied this same standard to ML recipe changes, data mixture changes, and numerics changes. Periodically, we bundled many proposals and trained the next-largest tier of the ladder, establishing new baseline if the scaling projection passed validation. This allowed us to discover interactions between data, recipe, and implementation early; re-establish baselines for fast iteration; and collect intermediate feedback on the impact of the latest pretraining recipe on the midtraining and post-training workflows. Data-Limited Subsampling. For scaling-ladder ablations to predict improvements at the target scale, smaller tiers must reflect the data constraints of the final pretraining run. The target run repeats some datasets many times to pad its token horizon and re-expose the model to selected valuable training data. In the ladder, smaller model tiers are trained on shorter horizons, and scaling down the mixture naïvely would make them train on unique tokens instead. This setup would not accurately model the effect of data repetition in the target model, and would not project its effect across the scaling ladder tiers. Following Muennighoff et al. [25], we applied the procedure we coined data-limited subsampling (DLS) to include these effects in the scaling ladder. For each tier, we reduced the available data in proportion to the number of training tokens. This kept the number of passes through each source approximately equal to that of the final training run. This makes the tradeoff between data quality and quantity visible throughout the ladder and helps distinguish improvements that transfer to the final training regime from those that depend on access to fresh data. Scaling Laws As our ladder varies the active parameters and the token horizon, we fit scaling law to predict the peak learning rate and weight decay for each ladder tier. We used multiplicative form following Bjorck et al. [26], which suggests that the active parameters, batch size, and token horizon dependencies can be isolated. Our peak learning rate and peak weight decay scaling law takes the functional form: max(𝑁, 𝐷, 𝐵) = 𝐶𝜂 𝑁𝛼𝜂 𝐷𝛽𝜂 𝐵𝛾𝜂 , 𝜂 𝜆 max(𝑁, 𝐷, 𝐵) = 𝐶𝜆 𝑁𝛼𝜆 𝐷𝛽𝜆 𝐵𝛾𝜆 Here, 𝑁 is the number of active non-embedding parameters, 𝐷 the token horizon, and 𝐵 the batch size. We keep 𝐵 explicit because it varies across our ladder. For 𝛾𝜂 we use the exponent 0.5 following e.g. Malladi et al. [27], and for 𝛽𝜂 we use 0.32 following Bjorck et al. [26]. To keep the effective learning rate constant across parameters, when varying the batch size and the token horizon, we set 𝜆 𝜂2 to fix the exponents 𝛾𝜆 and 𝛽𝜆 to 1.0 and 0.64, respectively. With these exponents fixed, the constant term and the exponent for the model size, namely, 𝐶𝜂, 𝐶𝜆, 𝛼𝜂, 𝛼𝛾, are the only remaining degrees of freedom. We fit these four terms by using linear regression data collected from extensive hyperparameter sweeps conducted at the lower tiers of our ladder. The tuning procedure is detailed in Appendix A, with scaling results in Figure 72. (2.7) Scaling Results. We validated our scaling recipe on the ladder using diverse in-house code and web validation sets, with all training data decontaminated against them. As shown in Figure 3, the recipe scales predictably across four orders of magnitude in compute: Beam Base matched its predicted performance and matched or outperformed the comparable open-source base models evaluated. 2.2 Data Beam is pretrained on 23.8T diverse high-quality tokens, packed into sequences of 16,384 tokens each. Average epochs is the ratio of training tokens to unique tokens. 2.2.1 Web Data Curation Preprocessing. Our web data is sourced from mixture of third-party providers and high-value subset of Common Crawl, comprising 245B raw HTML pages. We parsed each page with proprietary parser that preserves mathematical and code content that open-source parsers not optimized for pretraining use cases often corrupt or drop. We applied exact deduplication using an MD5 hash of the parsed text, resulting in 97B surviving documents. We then enriched each document with heuristic quality signals and learned classifier scores that support flexible selection throughout the downstream pipeline. The initial set of quality signals is listed in Appendix C. Domain Partitioning. MassiveWeb-style heuristic filters are commonly applied near the start of web-data curation pipelines [2832]. At their canonical thresholds, however, we found that they remove substantial amounts of high-quality technical content. We instead partitioned the pool by domain and apply domain-specific filtering pipelines. We partitioned the pool into five domains: math, code, STEM, English, and non-English. We trained three lightweight classifiers [33, 34] to score each documents relevance to the technical domains. To maintain high precision across 97B diverse, unfiltered web documents, we iteratively refined them using examples where their predictions disagreed with an internally configured judge models. We routed documents through fixed-priority cascade (math, code, then STEM), assigning each to the first domain whose score exceeded its threshold. We split the remaining documents into English and non-English partitions Beam Model Technical Report, Reflection Team et al. Figure 4: Web data curation from Common Crawl and third-party crawls through domain-specific filtering and quality partitioning. Technical domains are partitioned early and treated separately thereafter. using fastTexts lid-176 language identifier. Each partition was then fuzzy-deduplicated against itself using the deduplication pipeline described in Section 2.2.4. Table 4 reports token volume before and after deduplication. We omit the non-English partition from the discussion because it was processed separately using similar curation procedures. To test whether domain partitioning preserves technical data that standard unpartitioned pipeline would discard, we applied the canonical MassiveWeb filters to the curated technical datasets in our final mixture. Across webSTEM, web-code, and web-math, these filters would remove 8088% of tokens in each domain, totaling roughly 1.8T tokens, or 13% of the mixtures 13.73T unique tokens. Domain-Specific Curation. Every filtering decision trades corpus quality against token volume (Figure 5). For filter 𝐹 applied to pool 𝐷, let 𝑟tok(𝐹) denote the fraction of token mass removed and let 𝑞tok(𝑆) denote the Beam Model Technical Report, Reflection Team et al. token-weighted mean judge score of subset 𝑆. We define filter efficiency as 𝑒(𝐹) = 𝑞tok(𝐷keep) 𝑞tok(𝐷) 𝑟tok(𝐹) . (2.8) Random removal has expected efficiency zero, while removing documents in increasing judge-score order traces the oracle envelope. To obtain these scores, we used an internally configured judge models with handwritten, domain-specific prompt to score uniform random sample of thousands of documents per domain from 04, similar to FineWeb-Edu [31]. To discover filters for each domain, we began with basic document-length and mean-word-length filters, then extended the pipeline through the following iterative search-and-review loop: 1. Enumerate oneand two-condition rules over quantile grid of continuous signals and the discrete labels of categorical signals, then measure each rules marginal token-weighted efficiency on the current survivors. 2. Inspect the documents that each leading candidate would remove and retain, then select rule, sometimes adjusting its threshold or choosing candidate below the top-ranked rule. 3. Apply the selected rule and remove the matched documents from the active sample. 4. Repeat until the marginal efficiency of the remaining candidates no longer justifies further removal. The resulting domain-specific heuristic pipelines reduced total unique token volume to 19.5T, excluding the non-English partition. We then trained English web, STEM, and code quality classifiers and used them in second filtering stage. English and STEM applied threshold to their quality scores; code applied compound rules whose heuristic conditions fired only when quality score was also low; math received no classifier-based filtering. All token volumes are reported in trillions. Quality Classification. Our downstream quality-aware upsampling procedure assigns different weights to fine-grained quality tiers, thus the classifier must rank documents reliably across its full score range rather than merely separate highfrom low-quality data. We first evaluated two widely used open-source classifiers, DCLM [30] and FineWeb-Edu [31], on the hand-curated binary evaluation in Table 5. They obtained AUCs of 0.65 and 0.52, respectively. Agreement with human judgments does not necessarily predict downstream compute efficiency, so we subsequently evaluated each classifier on both judgment agreement and data ablations; their weak agreement nonetheless motivated training our own. We used downstream data ablations as the primary evaluation, supported by three cheaper classifier-level evaluations: 1. Data Ablation (Primary): We used each classifier to partition fixed English web corpus into tokenweighted quality tiers, apply common exponential quality upsampling schedule matched to the final designs mean repeat rate and effective-token budget, and train scaling ladder. Compute-efficiency differences isolated the ranking induced by the classifier. 2. Natural Holdout: We report Keep-AUC, the ROC-AUC for predicting the judges binary keep label, on sample of documents from the natural web distribution excluded from classifier training. 3. Binary Evaluation: An small, adversarial set of web documents with unambiguous binary quality labels, hand-selected to probe specific failure modes (e.g. well-written documents on taboo subject matter). Beam Model Technical Report, Reflection Team et al. Figure 5: Data curation as quality-volume tradeoff. The x-axis shows cumulative tokens removed, and the y-axis shows the token-weighted mean judge quality of the retained data. Each curve progressively removes documents in ascending order of an individual quality signal, while markers show complete multi-rule filter pipelines. Random removal preserves mean quality in expectation (gray dashed line), and removal in ascending judge-quality order defines the oracle upper envelope. 4. Ordinal Evaluation: pairwise-comparison tournament, run by an internally configured oracle judge model, produced reference ranking over roughly 100 held-out documents; classifiers are scored by rank agreement (Spearman) against it. We developed binary quality judge using strong LLM and handwritten prompt. After tuning primarily against external development examples to limit overfitting to the binary evaluation, the final judge reached Cohens kappa of 0.82 on that evaluation. We then labeled several hundred thousand documents selected from 522M-document sample using weighted reservoir sampling over document format, topic, and weak quality score from prior internal quality classifier. The format and topic labels are supplied by internally developed WebOrganizer-style taxonomy classifiers [35]. The best-performing sampling recipe preserved natural-distribution backbone while upweighting rare formats and documents assigned mid-range or high scores by the prior classifier. Finally, we used the labels to train an in-house small classifier. Table 5 reports the three classifier-level evaluations. We also trained fastText classifier on the same labels. Classifier arms use common quality upsampling schedule; DCLM fastText defines the 1.0 baseline. uniform-sampling control over the retained quality tiers from our classifier isolates the schedules contribution. STEM and code validation serve as expected-neutral controls because only English web data differs. fixed and optimize the upsampling schedule. Using our final quality classifier, we partitioned the corpus into quality tiers and study both choices with scaling-ladder ablations. We first retained the top 𝑁 quality tiers and sample uniformly from them, increasing their repeat rate as 𝑁 decreases to fill the fixed effective-token budget. The best measured setting shifts from retaining the top three quality tiers at the smallest tested scale to the top six at the largest scales, suggesting that the optimal retained fraction widens with scale. Because the production horizon substantially exceeds the largest scale tested in this sweep, we erred toward broader coverage and retained the top nine quality tiers, or 45% of web tokens. Fixing the top nine quality tiers, we swept several quality upsampling schedules and selected the strongest: truncated-exponential taper capped at approximately 2 repetition with mean repeat rate of approximately 1.5. Our final schedule yields roughly 10% higher compute efficiency than uniform sampling. Multilingual Data Curation. Our non-English partition followed the same high-level curation approach, using GlotLID [36] for language identification and language-aware variants of the filtering and quality-scoring stages in Section 2.2.1. 2.2.2 Code Data Curation The code corpus comprises three categories: source code files, source code notebooks, and web-code documents. Web-code processing is described in Section 2.2.1. Below, we detail the processing of source code and notebooks. Enrichment. We first enriched all files with metadata and quality signals. We used go-enry [37] and Magika [38] for language detection, chardetng [39] for encoding detection, and additional detectors for licenses, binary content, generated code, and vendored dependencies. We removed files with restrictive licenses and oversized files, then perform exact deduplication using Git blob content hashes. When identical files occur in multiple repositories, we preferentially retained the copy from the repository with more stars and forks, followed by deterministic tie-breakers. Notebooks. We separated notebooks from ordinary source code files because notebooks are often experimental working documents rather than polished software artifacts. They commonly contain exploratory work, repeated or partially executed code, prose, and embedded media, making them noisier and less structurally consistent than source code files. Moreover, notebooks are stored natively in verbose JSON container format, to which ordinary source-code filters cannot be applied reliably. We parsed each notebook and convert its cells, in their original order, into deterministic script-like representation. We removed cell outputs, discarded empty cells, and replaced media references with compact textual placeholders. Malformed notebooks that cannot be repaired and parsed are excluded. 15 Beam Model Technical Report, Reflection Team et al. Curation. Next, we applied separate, multi-step filtering pipelines to conventional source-code files and notebooks to remove low-quality, unlearnable data. Source Code: We identified and removed files containing automatically generated code markers or originating from vendored dependencies. We also removed binary-like files, highly compressible files dominated by repetitive content, and structured noise such as hexadecimal and hash dumps, Intel HEX and Motorola S-record files, numeric and metrics tables, serialized pickle data, OCR markup, subtitles, repeated digit-heavy tables, and documents with high fraction of non-printable characters. We then examined the distributions of curation signals separately for each programming language and use these distributions to establish language-specific thresholds for minimum and maximum file size, minimum alphabetic-character ratio, and maximum line length. Notebooks: We examined the distributions of notebook-specific signals and establish separate thresholds for minimum and maximum document size, minimum number of lines, maximum line length, minimum alphabetic-character ratio, compressibility, and the presence of encoded data. Adjust Language Distribution. Finally, we inspected the corpus distribution and deterministically downsample overrepresented languages and artifact-heavy file categories, including markup and configuration formats, generated stubs, IDE-generated files, and framework-specific assets. 2.2.3 STEM and PDF Data Curation PDF documents are large fraction of our training corpus. We converted the PDF documents to structured text with an OCR model operated as horizontally scaled Ray pipeline over GPU clusters. Downstream of OCR, conversion and quality layer turns per-page structured output into complete documents, with dedicated detectors for degenerate model output, blank or uninformative pages, and incomplete documents. High-Level Architecture Figure 7 illustrates the pipeline: controller plus fleet of mini-clusters. The controller is single Ray/KubeRay process per run that owns the workset, decides how work is partitioned, launches and monitors mini-clusters, and reconciles what finished against what was assigned. Each mini-cluster is self-contained Ray cluster that processes one slice of the corpus to completion and is torn down. Colocating CPU and GPU Workloads. mini-cluster maps to given GPU node (H100, H200, RTX Pro 6000, etc). Both rendering and OCR run on the same nodes: the render workers (CPU actors) are co-located with the GPU actors, so nodes CPUs are rendering the next documents while its GPUs are transcribing pages that are already rendered. Since transcribing takes twice as long as rendering, and with roughly hundred render workers feeding eight GPUs per node, the GPUs set the nodes ceiling. We feed the GPUs through bounded queues with backpressure detection, throttling rendering when they fill and draining stalled work when they starve, so that the GPUs stay saturated and every available GPU-second goes to transcription. OCR Internals. render worker takes whole document, then validates, and rasterizes it into pages. Rendered pages from many documents are interleaved in the GPU queue and packed into batches. The structured OCR output (Figure 8) is then reassembled per document: documents pages are written back to storage only once every one of them has been transcribed, so downstream consumers never see partially processed document. Failures follow the same shape: problematic page fails alone and is recorded as such, and document is dead-lettered only when its page failures exceed per-document budget. Serving Optimizations OCR runs on vLLM as an in-process engine inside each GPU actor. Because OCR is the bottleneck, two changes to how the engine is driven account for most of the serving-side throughput gain, and both were accepted on controlled measurements. Per-Accelerator Tuning via Parameter Sweep. The serving parameters that govern occupancy (admission width, page-pipeline depth, and the prefill token budget) interact with each other and with the accelerators memory and compute shape, so single global default leaves throughput on the table on every node type. We tuned them empirically per accelerator class on production hardware: we performed parameter sweep for each 16 Beam Model Technical Report, Reflection Team et al. Figure 7: Scalable OCR and document curation. run controller assigns work to warm Ray mini-clusters; co-located CPU rendering and GPU OCR actors process pages before document assembly and curation. accelerator (H100, RTX Pro 6000, H200, etc) to identify the correct parameter values that will maximize the throughput for said accelerator. Reliability and Auto Remediation Pages Whose Prompt Exceeds the Models Context: Very tall or very dense pages produce more vision tokens than the context allows. Pages are now pre-validated from their image headers against the models own processor geometry, with threshold deliberately looser than the engines so page the engine would accept is never refused, and any rejection that still reaches the engine evicts the largest page and retries until the batch settles. Long Skinny Pages: Images with aspect ratio above 200:1 (for example an 81650 strip) make the vision processors resize routine raise unconditionally, deterministically poisoning any batch they join. Rejected terminally at pre-validation. Decompression Bombs: Images whose decoded size exceeds the imaging librarys pixel limit fail on every load attempt. Rejected terminally at pre-validation. Large PDFs: We found PDFs that are many thousands of pages to usually be very low quality, so we pre-filter them to reduce compute waste and improve processing throughput. Failure Handling. Failure is inevitable due to the scale at which we operate. The pipeline was therefore designed to absorb failures as they come, catching and containing failures at the smallest possible granularity and page level. There are three main classes of failure: Page Level: Every page is its own inference request. After three failed retries, page is classified as failed. Document Level Due to Page Failure: If document has more than two pages that have run out of retries, the entire document is marked as failed and is removed from downstream processing. 17 Beam Model Technical Report, Reflection Team et al. Figure 8: Example of structured OCR output. The input page and detected regions are shown alongside the rendered HTML, preserving text, tables, and equations. Defective Documents: Documents that are deemed unsuitable (corrupt, encrypted, or over the page limit) go to dead-letter table with specified reason listed. As part of failure handling, we keep thorough record of each action. Each document writes status events to status tracking table with the attempt number, final status, and error code. Each page row records whether OCR succeeded, the error code if it did not, and how long it took. Granular record keeping adds resiliency by allowing long running OCR jobs to continue from where they left off in the event of failure. Post-Processing Figure 9 shows all the quality checks and processes that we have once OCR is done. The goal of post-processing is to ensure that low quality and malformed data does not enter our pretraining corpus. Quality issues can arise from different sources: low quality source, OCR processing artifacts. Low Quality Source. The PDF itself could be relatively low signal for text model. Content targeted at children with large number of pictures and limited vocabulary is one example. To address this, we employed custom filters for minimum number of words per page. 18 Beam Model Technical Report, Reflection Team et al. Figure 9: Document post-processing: HTML-to-Markdown conversion, completeness checks, page-quality filtering, ordered assembly, and document-level quality checks. OCR Processing Artifacts. We observed that VLM-based OCR is prone to repetition loops, especially when input pages are unclear or blank. To fix this, we developed series of page-level filters we describe below. Panels and of Figure 10 are types of repetitions that we observe from VLM-powered OCR model. Repetition Detector. VLM-based OCR occasionally enters degenerate generation loops, particularly on blank, degraded or content-rich pages. We detected these failures with section-aware logistic regression model over features derived from both the generated text and its document structure. These features measure compressibility, repeated substrings, repeated token sequences, repeated lines and table rows, and token n-gram duplication. We also include features for non-exact loops, such as implausibly long sequences of increasing numbers. Figure 11 summarizes the detector, and Table 6 lists its numeric signals. Because genuine repetition failures are rare, uniformly sampled evaluation set would contain too few positive examples to measure recall reliably. We therefore oversampled pages from relevant content types and repetitionrisk ranges, then weighted each example by the inverse of its sampling probability when computing aggregate metrics. This gave us enough failure cases to evaluate the detector while keeping the reported results representative of the full corpus. 19 Beam Model Technical Report, Reflection Team et al. Figure 10: Schematic examples of (A) exact text repetition, (B) runaway counting, and (C) legitimate repeated structure. These illustrate feature families, not production pages or measured classifier decisions. Figure 11: Repetition detection combines text-derived numeric features with the dominant HTML region type. section-specific logistic model and configured rules determine whether to flag page. Judged against an evaluation set sampled from our data, the detector caught 99.3% of severe repetition cases. We achieved 89.5% precision and 92.0% recall overall, while falsely flagging only 0.06% of clean pages. Table 7 reports both page filters. Blank Page Filtering. Furthermore, we filtered pages that are blank or whose print is too faded to recover reliably. We make this decision from the rendered page image rather than the OCR output, since the model can sometimes generate text even when the input page is empty. To balance the needs of scale, we leveraged fast computer vision signals including image contrast, Maximally Stable Extremal Regions (MSER), and Sauvola adaptive binarization to search for connected components resembling printed characters. The combination of these 3 signals allowed us to reach 98.2% precision and 96.5% recall, while incorrectly filtering only 0.06% of clean pages. OCR Confidence. Each page produced by the OCR model includes confidence score. We aggregate these scores at the document level and filter documents whose average confidence is below 0.8. This removes documents where the transcription is broadly unreliable. 20 Beam Model Technical Report, Reflection Team et al. Signal family Computed measure Decision role Compressibility (1) Repeated substrings (1) Consecutive repetition (3) Row repetition (2) Token n-grams (2) Counter templates (extension) Counting progressions (extension) Minimum compressed / original byte ratio over text suffixes. Longest repeated-substring fraction after digit masking; first 16K characters. Longest runs of identical lines, whitespace-delimited tokens and table cells. Most-common row fraction; 1 distinct rows / total rows. Frequency / token count for the most common word 2-gram and 4-gram. Longest normalized-line run and repeated-line share after masking counters. Longest same-prefix, constant-step integer run; text coverage of long runs. Logistic input + independent compression rule Logistic input Logistic inputs Logistic inputs Logistic inputs Additional logistic inputs when configured Separate run-length rule; coverage stored only Table 6: Numeric repetition signals. Parenthesized counts sum to nine core model inputs; extension rows are configuration-dependent. Detector Precision Recall Severe-case recall Clean-page FPR Repetition Blank page 89.5% 92.0% 98.2% 96.5% 99.3% 0.06% 0.06% Table 7: Corpus-weighted OCR page-filter evaluation. Low-Information Page Classifier. Some pages are transcribed correctly but contain little self-contained information such as indexes, bare reference lists and predominantly decorative pages. We used an LLM judge to label examples at scale, then train fastText classifier on the resulting labels. The classifier uses the normalized page text together with coarse start, middle, or end position signal. Essentially, this classifier ensures we increase the information density of our corpus instead of wasting compute on boilerplate and low-information pages. Document Assembly HTML-to-Markdown Conversion. Our VLM-based OCR model returns structured HTML for each page. We converted it to Markdown, removing page headers and footers while preserving elements such as equations, tables, code, lists, and footnotes. Page Aggregation. We first checked that all expected pages are present and that none are partial or failed. Pages flagged as repetitive, blank, or low-information are excluded, and the rest are stitched together in order. We discarded the entire document if more than 10% of its pages contain repetition. Blank and low-information pages do not count toward this threshold. Document-Level Filtering. Finally, we removed documents with low OCR confidence, too little text, or too few characters per page. This catches image-heavy and otherwise sparse documents that contain little useful training content. Key Results of Quality Improvements Under controlled experiments, we found that improving document quality and post-processing techniques produced gains comparable to increasing data volume. The benefits were most pronounced on mathematics and STEM tasks and were consistent across multiple evaluations. Within the range tested, we did not observe clear diminishing returns from adding more high-quality documents. These results suggest that better filtering and data selection are as important as corpus scale. 21 Beam Model Technical Report, Reflection Team et al. 2.2.4 Deduplication and Decontamination Across all pretraining data pipelines we applied single, unified deduplication process to remove exact and near-duplicates within individual sources and across the entire data mixture. We designed this pipeline with recall and speed/scale as first-class constraints, and we accept some false positives at scale. This let us run the pipeline regularly as new data is sourced or new ablations start. The pipeline has three stages: (a) an initial exact-deduplication step based on content hashing, (b) cheap MinHash-based fuzzy prefilter that generates candidate clusters and duplicate pairs, and (c) precision filter using Levenshtein-style edit distance that narrows matches based on token similarity, rank, and order. For fuzzy matching, we represent each document using overlapping token n-grams and compute compact MinHash signatures. Locality-sensitive hashing groups documents with similar signatures, avoiding an exhaustive comparison of every document pair. We then compared candidate pairs using normalized token-level edit distance, which accounts for insertions, deletions, and substitutions. When pair meets the similarity threshold, we remove the lower-ranked document according to configured source priorities, document quality, and deterministic tie-breaking rules. To bound computation on highly repetitive clusters and very long documents, some cases used rank-based removal without full edit-distance verification. We separately decontaminated training data against designated evaluation and validation collections. This check measures the fraction of an evaluation samples distinct token n-grams that appear in training document. Using evaluation-side containment allowed us to detect evaluation text embedded in much longer document without diluting the match with unrelated surrounding content. After ablations on both precision and recall of decontamination, we chose to use overlapping token 13-grams and remove training document if it contains at least 30% of the distinct 13-grams of any indexed evaluation or validation sample. We also implemented number of infrastructure optimizations so that each stage can be horizontally scaled as far as needed with minimal map-reduce -style coordination, and we rely on object storage as cheap backend. Together, these let us use CPU machines across most providers and instance shapes and be fault-tolerant if capacity is preempted or individual tasks fail. 2.2.5 Data Materialization and Packing Offline Materialization We materialize all pretraining data offline: dedicated data job compiles the weighted document mixture into an immutable artifact of fixed-length 16K training sequences, in exact training order, with every token span carrying provenance to its source document. The training loop performs no sampling, mixing, shuffling, or packing of its own. This buys three properties. Immutability: the data is frozen before the first step and cannot drift with input-pipeline changes, worker scheduling, or restarts. Reproducibility: every run and restart consumes data in identical order, keeping run-to-run variance controlled. Verifiability: the full artifact exists before training, so an independent offline job validates provenance, realized mixture ratios, token accounting, and shuffle quality before any accelerator time is committed; the final artifact for this run passed all such checks. Tail-Patching. The same contract makes continued pretraining tractable. When valuable new data lands after run is underway, we tailpatchpreserve the consumed prefix exactly, let untouched sources continue their epochs, and materialize only the future suffix under an updated mixture. The materialized data is bitwise equivalent to what run planned on the new mixture from that point would have consumed. Packing We pack using the concat-then-split (CtS) algorithm: documents are concatenated, separated by single EOS at each documents true end, and split into fixed 16K sequences. Within packed sequence, we also assign segment IDs that mark document boundaries, reset positions at each document boundary, and loss-mask the first token of new document. Sources that already arrive as coherent sequence-length chunks pass through unchanged; everything else is packed at the document level. This enables document-level attention masking, so that each token attends only to tokens within its own document. 22 Beam Model Technical Report, Reflection Team et al. The variant of concat-then-split used in our pipeline we coin split-shuffle packing (SSP). It addresses the main packing hazard of CtSlong documents that are packed continuously. One document can dominate several adjacent batches, visible at scale as periodic loss dips and gradient-norm spikes, and fixed cut points re-expose exactly the same windows on every repeat epoch. SSP addresses both issues. Long documents are cut into sequence-length pieces with deterministic, per-epoch randomized boundaries, and the pieces are dispersed by strong global shuffle before packing. That way, SSP changes local batch composition without changing the selected document mixture. Matched SSP-versus-baseline training ablations at smaller ladder tiers showed smoother gradient-norm traces, lower loss variance, and small compute efficiency improvement. Data-Limited Subsampling (DLS). We applied the DLS subsampling procedure, described in Section 2.1.3, before SSP. Given source, seed, epoch, and target ratio, DLS deterministically permutes logical document identifiers and selects the required portion. The same configuration therefore produces the same membership independent of loader parallelism or storage partitioning. Selecting before splitting also means that document is sampled as one semantic unit rather than in proportion to the number of chunks it produces. For the scaling ladder, epoch-0 selections are nested across tiers: the documents used by smaller tier are contained in the corresponding larger-tier selection. Moving up the ladder adds data instead of replacing one random subset with another, making tier comparisons easier to interpret. Mixture sizing uses exact selected-token counts, rather than only document counts, to determine source repeats and the final partial epoch.

sections.title: 3 Midtraining
sections.content: Our midtraining stage focuses on sharpening the knowledge, reasoning, and core capabilities that allow Beam to perform agentic tasks. We divide midtraining into two stages. Stage 1 focuses on developing the core logical and reasoning capabilities of the model by training on 850B tokens at 32K context length. Stage 2 extends the context length to 512K tokens using an additional 100B training tokens. 3.1 Optimization We used sawtooth schedule for training hyperparameters in midtraining. We linearly warm up the learning rate from zero to the peak value, after which it follows the tail phase of the cosine scheduler curve used in pretraining. We reset the optimizer state at the start of each stage and warm up the learning rate to allow the optimizer moments to adapt to the new data distribution, keeping weight decay constant during warmup. After warmup, we scaled the weight decay by the square of the cosine-tail learning-rate schedule, following the AdamC methodology [22]. We conducted sweeps on the peak LR and found 5% of maximum pretraining learning rate to balance forgetting and learning in the midtraining stages. 3.2 Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) Training Health Our data distribution in midtraining differs from pretraining because it assigns greater weight to specialized domains like STEM and coding. As result, the token distribution per batch shifts between these two training stages, which affects the expert load balancing in MoE layers. We observed that enforcing expert balancing via the same expert bias and auxiliary loss recipes used in pretraining can hinder specialization and lead to lower model performance overall. To allow for expert specialization, we disabled router z-loss, sequence aux loss, and expert bias update. Empirically, updating router weights was sufficient to stabilize the MoE during midtraining, as measured by expert loads and router probabilities for the selected experts. To ensure expert diversification, we also track router weight rank and per-token entropy of the router probabilities. 3.3 Sequence Packing We found that it is beneficial to preserve full data samples during training and prevent splitting data between consecutive sequences within batch. We therefore used filter-best-fit packing algorithm for offline data preparation. This algorithm keeps documents whole, filters out oversized documents, then places remaining ones in bin with the least remaining space that still fits it. When document fits no bin, all occupied bins are emitted and padded to fixed length. Figure 12 shows the four steps in the algorithm: filtering, best-fit selection, flushing, and reset/finish. We still use document-level attention masking as in pretraining to limit attention only within each documents tokens. 23 Beam Model Technical Report, Reflection Team et al. Figure 12: This figure demonstrates an overview of the filter-best-fit algorithm. Oversized documents are first filtered out, then group of bins is allocated for packing. Each sample is assigned to the bin with the tightest fit. If no fit is found, the group is flushed and new set of empty bins are allocated. The process continues until all data is exhausted. We adopted Unicron (Section 6) with FlashAttention-4 [40] with zigzag-style sequence reordering for efficient (long-context) training. When used with context parallelism, our attention kernel enforces certain constraints on the length of the packed sequence as well as the length of each document. We address these constraints by adding padding tokens to each document whenever necessary during the offline packing. Padding enters the packed batches from two sources: the flushing step of the packing algorithm and the kernelalignment constraints above. Depending on the datas structure and length distribution, the resulting padding can be non-trivial, and these tokens are no-ops for training. We patched Megatron [41] to mask padding tokens from expert routing in the MoE layers, which saves computation and avoids expert overload and imbalance. 3.4 Data Ablation Methodology The midtraining mixture includes many small datasets that span different domains, sources, and quality tiers. To derisk each individual data source and guide our final data mixture composition, we conducted iterative ablations at smaller scale using smaller models and shorter token horizons. These proxy training runs allow us to examine how mixture selection, data quality, and training format affect both training dynamics and downstream performance, informing decisions for large-scale runs. All proxy runs use consistent mixture recipe. For each ablation, we draw 50% of the data from the stable mixture used in the previous large-scale run and 50% from the new source under ablation. This allows us to ablate individual sources and also identify undesirable interactions between data and capabilities early on. We enforce determinism in our training, which allows us to carefully study and diagnose the source of training instability manifested as spikes in loss and gradient norm in our ablations. Aside from hardware and modeling issues, we used spike analysis as tool to investigate bad data and flag batches for targeted inspection. Repeating this methodology of data cleaning across our ablations allowed us to create customized data filters to catch 24 Beam Model Technical Report, Reflection Team et al. Figure 13: This figure demonstrates the midtraining data curation pipeline. The seed pool feeds preparation and generation stages. Candidate examples are assessed using source references and independent checks, then accepted, discarded, or returned for refinement. This shared generate-assess-refine loop supports task synthesis, trace generation and rewriting, and instructional content generation. corrupted content, malformed formatting, excessive repetition, and preprocessing errors across wide variety of our data sources and domains. 3.5 Stage 1 Data The final Stage 1 midtraining mixture comprised 90% new data and 10% high-quality pretraining data retained for recall, with the latter helping to preserve base knowledge and regularize against overfitting as the model acquired new capabilities. By target token share, the full midtraining data mixture comprised 15% general knowledge, 30% advanced and intermediate STEM, and 45% coding skills, spanning competitive programming, basic software engineering, and terminal usage. The following subsections describe each component. Our data pipelines in Stage 1 were aimed at teaching the model specific, often niche behaviors and skills. Figure 13 shows high-level view of the common structure behind these pipelines. Starting from real, licensed seed corpora, we passed them through sequence of transformation stages that re-express that source knowledge in many new formats: programmatically constructed tasks with verifiable answers, worked procedures, and dense knowledge documents. Many different open source models played distinct roles across the pipelinecurating and cleaning the seed pool, rewriting and reformatting content into varied surfaces and styles, solving tasks to produce ground truth when unavailable, verifying the quality of the final training data, and applying high-quality filteringso that no one models idiosyncrasies dominated the resulting data. Across the pipelines, we ensured the data was anchored to correct outcomes and grounded source knowledge. The midtraining data embedded various tool modalities like terminal interfaces or coding, as well as different problem-decomposition skills the model will need later, establishing strong base for exploration and solving complex reasoning tasks during agentic reinforcement learning. 3.5.1 STEM and Other Niche Knowledge To enhance Beams general reasoning and problem-solving capabilities, we created targeted corpus of data focused on STEM and selected topics in other disciplines, including the social sciences. The corpus spans broad range of 25 Beam Model Technical Report, Reflection Team et al. disciplines and levels of specialization, with particular attention to underrepresented subtopics and specialized technical material. Beyond topical coverage, we explicitly gathered data that leverages and showcases diverse problem-solving skills, including deriving results, explaining concepts, and implementing scientific methods. Seed Curation We curated seeds from technical web content like academic papers as well as licensed advanced textbooks. We classified documents by subject area and filtered for educational value and technical substance, prioritizing material containing substantive explanations, derivations, and problem-solving. Within each domain, we sought coverage of finer-grained subtopics using hierarchical subject labels. We organized these labels into knowledge graph, connecting broad disciplines to increasingly specialized subtopics and linking each topic to its associated source documents and seeds. This structure made coverage gaps and concentrations visible, supporting targeted curation of underrepresented areas and balanced sampling across related subtopics. Data Transformation model does not learn reasoning best from raw technical material like papers, or dense passages. We focused our efforts on reshaping the raw data into formats that make the reasoning and logic itself explicit. For research papers, we drew on derivations and calculations and recast them as self-contained tasks, supplying the needed context while withholding the target result, which surfaces specialized intermediate steps that research writing tends to skip. For multi-step problems, we used the knowledge graph and concept co-occurrence patterns to select related ideas. We then synthesized tasks with dependencies between steps and checked that the combined concepts and reasoning were coherent. This approach broadened conceptual coverage while keeping the synthesized tasks grounded in established problem structures. For explanatory material, we rewrote technical passages as tutorials and multi-turn discussions that mirror how reasoning actually unfolds, from decomposing problem to exploring approaches and revising when something doesnt hold up, giving content from varied sources clearer, more consistent presentation without losing technical substance. Together, these approaches turned source material into reasoning-rich training data that is grounded in real scientific work, broad in its concept coverage, and pedagogically clear. Quality Control and Refinement. We tailored quality checks to the type of examples and formatting applied to the source data. For any generated data, we used available source answers and derivations, and symbolic, numerical, or execution checks where applicable. Multi-hop tasks were also checked for correct intermediate results and meaningful dependencies between steps. For tutorials and discussions, LLM judges assessed technical accuracy, clarity, and fidelity to the source. After rewriting, we checked the text for remaining unwanted behaviors. Examples with errors, weak supporting evidence, or unwanted behaviors were repaired, rewritten, or regenerated while preserving style and necessary checks. Refinement can also increase task complexity by adding constraints or adding further dependent seeds and steps. Difficulty Calibration and Coding Integration. For portions of our data that have computational final answer, we used pass@k calibration to measure difficulty and select data samples near the models capability frontier: challenging enough to require substantive work from the model, while remaining within reach. Calibration was relative to the evaluated checkpoint and informed adjustments to task selection and formatting of the raw data as capabilities improved. Low solve rates also prompted checks for ambiguity or low quality of the training document due to lossy reformatting. We allowed Beam to also leverage written code as computational medium where reasoning alone tended to fail, thus allowing the model to reproduce the complex computations encountered in the source documents. 3.5.2 Competitive Programming Our data pipelines for competitive programming provide examples that emphasize algorithm selection, step-bystep reasoning, and reaching the correct implementation. These pipelines combine human-authored artifacts with model-generated supervision, emphasizing coverage, correctness, and useful training signals. Seed Curation Our competitive-programming data is curated from programming datasets, official contest archives, and repositoryderived algorithmic examples. We normalize these heterogeneous sources, reconcile overlapping records, and review statements for completeness and clarity. We audit all data for semantic contamination against coding 26 Beam Model Technical Report, Reflection Team et al. benchmarks that we use for signal. We use lexical checks as well as embedding-based comparisons to flag potential paraphrases, and use LLM-assisted review to assess whether training solution would solve an evaluation task with only mechanical changes. We organize the decontaminated seeds under topic hierarchy spanning dynamic programming, graph and string algorithms, advanced data structures, number theory, and geometry, with finer-grained techniques such as Digit DP, rerooting on trees, and rollback union-find. This hierarchy guides how we control diversity and expand the seed collection. Data Transformation Using the topic hierarchy over seeds, we expanded our training corpus by conditioning on topic and small set of relevant seeds to generate similarly structured problems, while reusing the reference solutions or an explanation of the underlying method. We vary difficulty, structure, programming language, and interface. Every problem, whether original or adapted, passes an LLM-assisted quality review covering clarity, internal consistency, difficulty, novelty, and learning value. Where tests or verification checks exist, solutions are run against them. Where only reference solutions exist, we built test suites from cases on which multiple solutions agree, and audit that trusted solutions pass and known-incorrect ones are rejected. Problems lacking both are solved via collection of different models and reviewed for correctness. Where reference solutions are available, we also rewrite them into tutorial-style documents covering the key observations, algorithms, correctness arguments, complexity analysis, and pitfalls, surfacing concepts that are only implicit in source code. 3.5.3 Software Engineering (SWE) This category of data teaches models the fundamental knowledge for understanding and improving codebases, extending their capability beyond code generation in isolation. The data broadly covers two complementary capabilities: repository understanding, which involves identifying relevant code and reasoning about its structure and behavior, and feature implementation, which involves translating natural-language requirements into concrete code changes. Together, these capabilities support the broader software engineering workflow, from understanding an unfamiliar repository to implementing and validating change. Seed Curation We constructed all software-engineering data from real GitHub repositories, drawing on issues, pull requests, and commit histories. Across all data pipelines, we first apply common set of repository filters: we exclude low-quality repositories, including those with few stars, no activity in recent years, or primarily non-code content. We remove repositories that are duplicated, have non-permissive licenses, or are benchmark-contaminated. From the remaining repositories, we further filter down the issues, commits, or pull requests (PRs) based on various heuristics of quality, completeness, complexity, and capability coverage. Data Transformations Repository-Level Understanding. One of the fundamental capabilities needed for software engineering is reasoning and understanding across files, interfaces, and dependencies. To build this capability in the model, we constructed targeted repository-understanding data grounded in real GitHub issues that call for explanation or analysis rather than implementation, covering topics such as design rationale, dependency relationships, feature extensibility, and data or control flow. We further expand this set by synthetically generating new questions that are attached to real code, broadening coverage beyond the distribution of organic issues. The entire pool is filtered to retain questions that are answerable, grounded in the in-context code, and non-trivial. We further produce design documents that describe the structure of code repos at multiple levels of abstraction. Together, these training samples help models reason about repositories as whole rather than individual code excerpts, enabling them to navigate unfamiliar codebases, connect information across files, and explain code structure and behavior. Feature Implementation. We built various forms of supervision from real repository history, focusing on building foundational SWE knowledge and skills at scale, and applying those skills through repository exploration and feedback-driven refinement. Starting from the retained seed commits, we reconstructed natural-language task from the commit description and code changes, and pair it with repository context assembled from the changed files and their dependencies. 27 Beam Model Technical Report, Reflection Team et al. We use LLM-assisted refinement to improve the reference changes and to produce accompanying rationales and explanations for the seed code patches. Finally, we reformat the training samples into several output styles, including unified diffs and Bash commands, so the model learns different code editing interfaces. We also create template data that teaches the model how to work with repository over multiple steps, including skills such as inspecting files, searching for definitions and usages, and applying edits as its understanding develops. In addition to commit data, we also created additional targeted data by removing selected functionalities in existing code and writing specifications for reconstructing it. Varying the scope of the removed code, from single functions to groups of files, yields tasks from localized edits to complex multi-file features. 3.5.4 Terminal Use We developed specific data pipelines to make the model familiar with problem solving using the terminal. The focus at the midtraining stage was to introduce broad horizon coverage of terminal related skills including shell scripting, systems programming, networking, data processing and more. Our pipelines are grounded in human written scenarios from our seed sources and are expanded to produce similarly diverse and realistic training examples. Seed Curation Our training data is grounded in real-world raw artifacts. This gives us two benefits: Distribution: Human-created issues, questions, and discussions capture the full spectrum of problems solved via terminal, including the long tail of flags, quoting mistakes, and environment quirks. Verifiability: post with an accepted answer gives us reference to grade against or concrete problem to turn into sandbox-checked task. We curated seeds from various available web sources and technical documentation like manual pages, --help, and library docs. For community sources, we retained only examples with accepted answers and removed low-quality or incomplete records, including those that depended on missing images. Separately, we collected thousands of documentation pages covering command-line tools, shell builtins, shell-language constructs, and Python libraries. We then create comprehensive taxonomy of all skillsets the model is required to have in order to solve terminal tasks. Data Transformation The first family of training documents is question-and-answer data built from community threads with accepted solutions. Each thread is rewritten into standalone question with its implicit assumptions made explicit, personal and site-specific context removed, and the original technical setting preserved. The rewrite is deliberately varied so it is never verbatim copy. Each question is then answered independently, without access to the accepted answer, and both the rewrite and the answer are scored for fidelity, correctness, completeness, and methodology. Answers that reach valid conclusion by different route than the original post are retained rather than discarded, while weak rewrites and incorrect answers are removed. The second family covers hands-on terminal work. Starting from the skillset taxonomies, we augment them with detailed metadata, such as what the skill teaches, canonical commands and their commonly used flags, and related Python packages. We also add verifier hints for writing tests that check outcomes rather than methods. We then pair each seed artifact with their related skill augmentations and expand them into many complete, executable tasks that include clear instruction, realistic workspace, setup procedure, an initial-state check, hidden final test, and reference solution. We control diversity of the training samples by covering various capability combinations and difficulty axes, such as hidden faults, distractors, or subtle traps. We apply two levels of quality control using 1) inexpensive static checks to catch obvious problems and mismatches with the original raw seeds, and 2) validation step in real environment to confirm that each task starts from valid state, fails when nothing is done, and passes once the reference solution is applied. 3.6 Stage 2 Data The Stage 2 mixture combined recall data from pretraining and Stage 1 with the following new data sources: Organic long-context data, such as books, research articles, and code repositories. This data naturally encodes long-range dependency, providing crucial signals for long-context learning. Repositories are 28 Beam Model Technical Report, Reflection Team et al. Figure 14: The final Stage 2 mixture balances improvements in long-context performance against regressions in other capabilities. The figure shows score differences relative to the Stage 1 checkpoint. carefully selected following natural programming language distribution. We pack the coding files in repository into single sequence based on their cross-file dependencies. Synthetic long-context data. We use mix of in-house and open-source datasets to enhance the models long-range retrieval and reasoning capability. The in-house portion is question-answer (QA) pairs generated from high-quality books across various domains with grounded context. We also adopt several open-license datasets such as LongCite [42], LongData, and LongAlign [43]. In experiments, we noticed that the mixing weight significantly affects the trade-off between long-context performance and other general model capabilities in the context extension stage: often, we saw consistent gains on long context benchmarks like RULER but with regressions of varying degrees on other benchmarks. Following grid search, we selected mixture of 50% organic long-context data, 15% synthetic long-context QA and instructionfollowing data, and 35% recall data from pretraining and Stage 1. This reaches reasonable balance as shown in Figure 14.

sections.title: 4 Post-Training
sections.content: Beams post-training pipeline combines two separately trained experts, an agentic expert and an alignment expert, through multi-teacher on-policy distillation (MOPD). Each expert undergoes short supervised fine-tuning (SFT) phase to establish response formats and tool-use syntax, followed by reinforcement learning (RL). This section describes our training approach, data generation and curation, and supporting infrastructure. 4.1 Agentic Expert We train the agentic expert to solve reasoning and long-horizon tasks across mathematics, STEM, competitive programming, software engineering, terminal use, web search, general tool use, and professional knowledge 29 Beam Model Technical Report, Reflection Team et al. work. Training consists of short supervised fine-tuning (SFT) phase followed by large-scale reinforcement learning (RL). SFT establishes the response and tool-call formats and seeds reasoning behaviors; RL develops these capabilities through interaction with tasks and environments. We first describe the training procedure and its empirical behavior, then detail the training data. 4.1.1 Supervised Fine-Tuning We initialize the agentic expert with short SFT phase focused on chat formatting, tool-call syntax, and reasoning behavior. We generate trajectories using an earlier version of our model on subset of the final task pool spanning all training domains. These trajectories are filtered for correctness and quality before being used for supervised training. 4.1.2 High-Compute Reinforcement Learning We train the agentic expert using GRPO-style policy-gradient method [44] in fully asynchronous setting. Asynchronous execution accommodates the wide variation in rollout durations, but introduces policy staleness as training proceeds while trajectories remain in flight. Stable optimization also requires consistency between training and inference, particularly in sampling and mixture-of-experts routing. Below, we describe our approach to these challenges, our reward design, and the resulting training dynamics and performance. Asynchronous rollouts. Agentic tasks produce heavy-tailed distribution of rollout durations. In our RL run, the median rollout completes in approximately 12 minutes, while roughly 2% take longer than an hour. For approximately one in five training steps, at least one contributing rollout took more than six hours. Waiting for all rollouts in each batch would therefore introduce substantial synchronization overhead. We decouple generation from optimization and update the inference workers after every optimizer step. In-flight rollouts continue under the updated weights without interruption, following the general approach of in-flight weight updates [45] and partial rollouts [46]. single trajectory may consequently span multiple policy versions. We record the policy version associated with each generated token. To accommodate differences in task duration, we use task-dependent rollout deadlines. Rollouts that exceed their deadlines are discarded, and rollout groups are retained only when enough rollouts have completed. Sampling consistency. Long trajectories create many opportunities to sample low-probability tokens. Such tokens can disrupt reasoning or invalidate tool calls, potentially derailing an otherwise successful trajectory. To reduce this risk, we use nucleus sampling with 𝑝 = 0.99 [47] and temperature set to 1.0. Nucleus sampling changes the behavior policy by truncating and renormalizing the token distribution. Computing full-vocabulary log-probabilities during training would leave this transformation unaccounted for and introduce gradients through tokens outside the sampled nucleus. Following the approach used in DeepSeek-V3.2 [48], we retain the nucleus 𝒩𝑡 used at each generation step and renormalize the training policy over that same set. This aligns the support used for generation and training, eliminating the mismatch due to applying different truncation masks. It does not eliminate differences caused by policy updates or numerical effects. Logits outside the recorded nucleus receive no direct gradient from the corresponding token-level objective. Routing and numerical consistency. Mixture-of-experts routing introduces another source of training inference mismatch: small numerical differences can change tokens top-𝑘 expert selection and therefore its subsequent computation. We use routing replay [49] to preserve the expert assignments made during generation. The inference engine records the selected experts for each token, and the trainer reuses those assignments while recomputing the gate values. Router weights and load-balancing biases remain frozen during RL. Although this fixes the router parameters, expert assignments can still change as the representations entering the router evolve, making replay relevant even with frozen router. To further reduce numerical discrepancies, we run the LM head, router, and residual stream in FP32 in both training and inference. Reward integrity. For software-engineering and terminal tasks, passing an automated verifier does not necessarily establish that solution is valid. model may modify tests, hard-code expected outputs, or exploit Beam Model Technical Report, Reflection Team et al. Figure 15: Optimization diagnostics during RL, including global gradient norm, per-token KL divergence between the sampling and training policies, and sampled-token negative log-likelihood. Shaded regions indicate training restricted to mathematics, STEM, and competitive programming (light), or software engineering (dark). weaknesses in the evaluation harness. We therefore apply judge2 with reward-hacking rubric to rollouts that pass their task verifier. Only the final patch was passed to the judge for evaluation. We additionally monitor the chain-of-thought of the model to detect hacking intention but do not apply direct optimization pressure to it. If the judge flags rollout as reward hacking, we set its correctness score to zero while retaining its length cost. Such rollout receives the same reward as failed attempt of equal length. The rubrics were updated during the run to track new reward hacks as the model discovered them. Training stability. Figure 15 summarizes the optimization dynamics.
