The gradient norm remains in narrow range without sustained drift, with median of 1.7103 and 99th percentile of 3.0103. The median per-token KL divergence between the sampling and training policies is 2.2 104 nats, and the mean absolute difference in token log-probabilities is 0.0085. Immediately after restart, when rollouts are generated using the current weights, the KL divergence is 8.7 105 nats. This provides reference for the remaining traininginference mismatch after sampling and routing replay. During asynchronous training, sampled tokens are on average five policy versions behind the trainer, introducing an additional source of divergence. The mean negative log-likelihood of sampled tokens increases gradually from 0.37 to 0.50 nats over the run. The trend differs by channel: for reasoning tokens, it rises from 0.63 to 0.69 nats, while for final-answer tokens it falls from 0.25 to 0.06 nats. These measurements show distinct changes in token predictability across channels, rather than uniform concentration of the policy. Response lengths remain broadly stable within each data-mixture phase. The mixture changes five times during training. Within phase, the median response length varies by at most one third; in phases from 52% of the run onward, it varies by less than 5%. Larger shifts coincide with changes in the mixture toward longer agentic tasks. Reasoning effort and length cost. We train the model to balance task performance against token use through an explicit reasoning-effort input and linear length penalty. The effort setting controls the rollout budget. Rollouts that exhaust this budget are terminated and receive no correctness reward. Among solutions with equal correctness rewards, the length penalty favors shorter responses. Varying the effort setting trains the model to adapt its token use to the requested budget. Performance and token efficiency. Figure 16 shows DeepSWE pass@1 as function of requested reasoning effort and realized output length. Relative to the SFT checkpoint, RL achieves higher performance at comparable output lengths and reaches comparable performance with fewer tokens. It also extends the range of effort levels over which additional computation improves performance. At 79% of the run, the model achieves 35% pass@1 at 𝑒 = 512. The final checkpoint continues to benefit from increasing effort through 𝑒 = 512, reaching 41% pass@1. more difficult set of software-engineering tasks is introduced at 83% of the run, between these checkpoints. These results demonstrate improvements in both token efficiency and the ability to use larger inference-time budgets effectively. 2In developing both the agentic and alignment experts, we made use of internally configured models which are variously referred to as graders, agents, and judges throughout this chapter. 31 Beam Model Technical Report, Reflection Team et al. Figure 16: DeepSWE pass@1 versus requested reasoning effort (left) and realized output length (right), for the SFT checkpoint and three RL checkpoints. RL improves the trade-off between performance and token use and extends the range of reasoning budgets over which performance continues to improve. The checkpoints at 39% and 79% of the run precede the introduction of more difficult software-engineering task set at 83%. Figure 17: Held-out evaluation scores during RL (pass@1, reasoning effort 512). Shaded regions mark phases that trained on single domain: mathematics, STEM and code only (light), and software engineering only (dark). BrowseComp measurements begin at 27% of the run, after change of search backend. Generalization. We evaluated checkpoints during the run on fixed suite of benchmarks whose tasks are excluded from the RL data. Each benchmark used the same settings throughout: temperature 1, top-𝑝 0.99, 𝑒 = 512 and 256K output limit (Figure 17). Scores improve steadily over the run. In two phases of the run, we trained on limited subset of domains: 2652% of the run used only mathematics, STEM and competitive programming, and 5265% used only software engineering. Figure 17 shows some of the evals across these phases. Software-engineering benchmarks held their level through the STEM-only phase, and STEM and coding benchmarks did not regress during the SWE-only phase. Skills also transferred across domains. The run trained on no search or browsing tasks before the 83% mark, yet BrowseComp improved from 50.1 at 27% to 57.9 at 83%. This demonstrates the generalization ability of Beam. Beam Model Technical Report, Reflection Team et al. 4.1.3 RL Task Curation Principles We sourced wide pool of several million verifiable RL tasks by drawing from open source repositories, purchasing them from vendors, or generating them synthetically with in-house pipelines. This broader pool was of variable quality and difficulty, and we aggressively filtered it down to nearly one million of the most difficult, high-quality tasks to support the final RL run. Across all domains, our approach to RL environment curation was one of first ensuring high bar for both the quality and difficulty of tasks. Then, given those constraints, we scaled to as many diverse tasks as possible to support large-scale RL. Our process was also iterative, after scaling we often filtered again based on our observations during RL. Quality. By quality, we mean tasks that have zero noise in their rewards. This means the tasks are not misleading (e.g., they should not be missing instructions or context, they should be well-formed, and the premise of the task should be sound), hackable (i.e., reward should be given only when the task is truly solved), or otherwise broken. Additionally, verifiers/reward functions must be robust and consistent. They should always give the same reward for the same answer. Some measures of quality are also model specific; for example, tasks where the model can give the correct answer without chain-of-thought, or in which successful hack was observed. Difficulty. By difficulty, we mean difficulty for training particular model. This means the task must neither be too hard (i.e., all or mostly zero rewards in group) nor too easy (i.e., all or mostly full rewards in group). Moreover, we work to ensure the task is not classified as too hard or too easy for the wrong reasons, such as: tasks where the answer is leaked in the question (making it seem artificially easy), evaluating the model with insufficient context (making it seem artificially hard), chat template formatting errors (masking the true difficulty), or impossible questions (which can lead to hacking behavior during evaluation, see [50]). In particular, there are long tail of domain-specific failure modes that can make tasks seem artificially hard, such as not being able to access particular website, overly strict memory/time requirements, and various sandboxing issues. Some of these are described in more detail below in the domain-specific sections. The sandbox services network controls are described in Section 6.6.5. Scale. We sourced tasks from open-source repositories, purchased them from vendors, or generated them from our own in-house synthetic pipelines. Existing open-source environments were valuable earlier in our development cycle; however, we found that when used in large-scale RL with performant model like Beam, they required extensive quality and difficulty filtering. Vendor-sourced tasks are high-quality and high-difficulty, but expensive. We found that developing our own in-house pipelines allowed us to satisfy the quality, difficulty, and scale requirements for large-scale RL on Beam. Diversity. To ensure the generality of our model, we curated tasks across wide diversity of task formats, programming languages, tool combinations, and topics. We applied the deduplication and decontamination procedure described in Section 4.1.4. Iterative Refinement. We considered our task pools to be ever-changing: following every round of experimentation, we analyzed rollouts and tried to understand if agent successes or failures could be attributed to issues in the tasks. For example, reward hacks newly observed in training run led to tasks being removed. Although the pool of tasks shrank over time, we converged on set that had the highest quality possible. 4.1.4 Deduplication and Decontamination Shared Sample Registration and Contamination Checks. For post-training task curation, we checked incoming training samples against shared collection of previously registered samples and excluded identified exact and near-duplicates from training. These checks addressed both repetition within the training data and contamination from evaluation samples. We used Jaccard similarity threshold of 0.95 for comparisons between training samples. When either sample belonged to an evaluation, we lowered the threshold to 0.80 to detect broader range of potential contamination. The following section describes the matching procedure. Scalable Duplicate Detection. We represented each sample as set of overlapping character 7-grams: every consecutive sequence of seven characters in its text. For two sets 𝐴 and 𝐵, Jaccard similarity measures the fraction of distinct n-grams shared by both samples relative to those present in either. Jaccard distance is one minus this 33 Beam Model Technical Report, Reflection Team et al. similarity: 𝐽(𝐴, 𝐵) = 𝐴 𝐵 𝐴 𝐵 , 𝑑𝐽(𝐴, 𝐵) = 1 𝐽(𝐴, 𝐵). Identical n-gram sets have distance zero; sets with no shared n-grams have distance one. Small edits can preserve much of the overlap, allowing detection of near-duplicates as well as exact copies. To avoid comparing every pair of samples, we used MinHash to summarize each n-gram set in compact signature and locality-sensitive hashing (LSH) to retrieve likely matches. This allowed searches over large collection without comparing each incoming sample directly with every stored example. We then calculated exact Jaccard similarity for each retrieved candidate and accepted match only when it met the relevant threshold. Guarantees and Limitations. MinHash LSH provides probabilistic retrieval: more similar pairs are more likely to be retrieved, but some pairs that meet the threshold may be missed. Exact verification ensures that accepted matches satisfy the similarity criterion; it does not guarantee that every near-duplicate is found. The method does not assess semantic similarity. Paraphrases, translations, and short questions embedded in much longer documents can have low Jaccard similarity. We therefore treat deduplication as practical but imperfect control on repetition and contamination. 4.1.5 Software Engineering (SWE) Training software engineering agents with reinforcement learning requires diverse repository-level tasks and reliable feedback on whether solution implements the requested behavior. We constructed executable environments from changes mined from software repositories and from synthetic feature-implementation tasks. Our approach combined environment reconstruction, behavioral verification, and task-quality assessment, building on recent work on scalable SWE environment construction [51, 52]. Task Curation Environment Construction. We used agents to turn mined repository changes into executable training tasks, drawing on methods for agentic environment construction described in SWE-Universe [53] and DockSmith [54]. Starting from the repository at its pre-change revision, an agent inspected the source and test patches, dependency manifests, and continuous integration configuration to discover the required dependencies, build steps, and affected tests. It specified the environment setup and wrote verifier, using execution feedback to diagnose failures and iteratively refine both. The agent packaged the resulting setup into reproducible container image which included problem statement, an executable repository snapshot, reference implementation, and verifier. We independently validated the constructed environment by running the verifier before and after the reference change, requiring it to fail before the change (fail-to-pass) and pass after it while rejecting observed regressions (pass-to-pass). We also revalidated tasks through the patch-submission and grading path used in training, including submission extraction and application in separate verifier environment. This checked that the task remained executable under the training environments resource and isolation constraints. Quality Filtering and Corpus Curation. Execution validity alone does not establish that task provides useful learning signalfor example, task prompts can be under-specified, making it difficult for an agent to solve the task in way that the verifier expects. We separately assessed specification clarity and test adequacy, properties also studied in SPICE [55] and SWE-rebench V2 [51]. The requested behavior had to be sufficiently specified by the problem statement and visible repository context (which we refer to as the solver-visible specification), and the verifier had to meaningfully test that behavior. Initial Static Validation. We developed judges to assess the problem statement, reference implementation, tests, and verification command against separate criteria. These models checked that: Statements describe an actionable change without leaking the solution or depending on unavailable attachments or discussions. Tests agree with the stated requirements, assert meaningful behavior, and permit equivalent correct implementations. Reference fixes are relevant to the requested change, and do not have hard-coded answers or modifications to test files. 34 Beam Model Technical Report, Reflection Team et al. Verifier commands do not manufacture success, suppress failures, or substitute superficial checks for behavioral tests. Repairable descriptions were rewritten and reassessed; tasks with unresolved integrity defects were excluded. Secondary Static Validation. second, stricter review examined whether (1) every tested requirement could be determined from the solver-visible specification, (2) whether the tests enforced the requested behavior, and (3) whether trivial or incomplete implementations could pass. The reference implementation was withheld from this assessment to avoid biasing the review with information unavailable to the solver. Each of these criteria received three independent model calls, with any valid negative judgment rejecting the task. Agentic Audits. We complemented artifact-based checks with agentic audits that inspected repositories, traced verification logic, and executed candidate implementations. Two judges assessed the agreement between the solver-visible specification and the verifier in complementary directions. The ambiguity judge checked whether the requirements enforced by the tests were justified by the specification. It looked for cases where the available information permitted multiple reasonable implementations, but the verifier accepted only some of them. The agent examined repository code, documentation, and established interfaces for context that resolved the apparent ambiguity. Where practical, the agent constructed and executed an alternative implementation to demonstrate that the verifier rejected behavior consistent with the visible specification. The verifier-strength judge checked whether the tests enforced the requested behavior. Before inspecting hidden tests or the reference implementation, the agent recorded the independently testable requirements established by the prompt and starting repository. It then mapped each requirement to the verification logic, checking whether violating that requirement would cause failure. The agent then attempted to generate incomplete or incorrect implementations that exploited gaps in verification. Such bypasses had to be discoverable from solver-visible information, rather than depend on privileged knowledge of hidden tests. Filtering and Rebalancing. Any tasks which failed to pass the static and agentic validation steps were discarded. We curated the resulting pool across programming languages and repositories, limited repeated variants of the same underlying change, and removed tasks that reference model solved reliably. We also excluded task identities and patch matches associated with held-out evaluations. These stages produced broad corpus of executable software changes spanning multiple language ecosystems. Task Pool. We curated an initial pool of candidate tasks, including those from our own pipeline, from proprietary vendor tasks, and from existing open-source SWE corpora: SWE-Gym [56], R2E-Gym [57], SWE-rebench V2 [51], Multi-SWE-RL [58], MEnvData [59], SWE-smith [60], and Scale-SWE [61]. We subsampled from this set by balancing programming languages and filtering for quality and difficulty. Figure 18 visualizes the distribution of subset of tasks from this final pool. Synthetic Feature-Implementation Tasks In addition to the pipeline described above, we found synthetic task generation to provide complementary way to expand the range of software changes available for training. We generated feature-implementation tasks by having an agent examine working repositorys documentation and source code. The agent identified substantial feature, and removed its implementation and associated tests. The removed behavior was specified as new implementation task and evaluated with hidden integration tests designed to permit alternative implementations. We required the remaining repository tests to pass after removal, and the feature verifier to fail without the feature and pass when the reference implementation was restored. This construction extended the task distribution to larger changes spanning multiple files and subsystems. Synthetic tasks received additional checks specific to feature removal. We inspected prompts for leaked implementation details, rebuilt derived artifacts from the modified repository, and scanned images for surviving copies of the removed code or tests. Adversarial agents attempted to recover leaked artifacts and use them to obtain passing result. Verifier guards also rejected unauthorized changes to test-selection configuration and import hooks. Tasks were required to pass three independent environment-validation trials under the training resource limits, excluding tasks with inconsistent outcomes. 35 Beam Model Technical Report, Reflection Team et al. Figure 18: Semantic Structure of the SWE Task Corpus. Each point represents task, positioned by t-SNE projection of embeddings of behavioral summaries and colored by programming language. Labels describe communities identified in the original embedding space. The figure shows 12K mined tasks and 1.5K synthesized feature tasks sampled from the full pool. Sample proportions do not represent final training-mixture weights; projected distances and areas are not quantitative measures of coverage or difficulty. Reward Hacking We also addressed reward hacking during training. To minimize the risk of hacking, the solvers submitted patch was evaluated in separate environment, preventing it from directly carrying changes to its execution environment into the verifier. We also cleaned repository images to remove post-change commit history and artifacts that could expose the reference solution. For submissions that passed the tests, an additional model-based judge examined the submitted code and verifier for evidence of reward hacking; submissions classified as successful hacks received zero reward. We additionally analyzed groups of rollouts for submission failures, inconsistent grades on identical or closely similar patches, and suspicious passing solutions. Task-health judges investigated whether groups with no 36 Beam Model Technical Report, Reflection Team et al. successful solutions reflected genuine difficulty, underspecified requirements, broken environments, or grading failures. Reward-integrity judges assessed whether successful solutions exploited test gaps or whether hidden tests required unsupported assumptions. These analyses supported ongoing diagnosis of task quality, complementing construction-time filtering and online reward checks. 4.1.6 Terminal Use Equipping an agent with bash toola single interface for executing arbitrary shell commandshas become the dominant way to give text-only language model autonomous control over computer. Through it, an agent can perform highly skilled work spanning software engineering, system administration, scientific computing, machine learning, and cybersecurity [62]. Task Curation We began by sourcing tasks both from vendors and our own synthetic pipelines, all following the Harbor format [63]. We also investigated open-source terminal-use tasks, but we found these did not meet our quality bar. Through our curation pipelines, tasks were filtered based on diversity, quality, and difficulty (described in the sections below). Diversity. With terminal agents operating across wide range of downstream tasks, we needed to ensure appropriate diversity in our training environments. We considered task diversity along three dimensions. These dimensions were used to develop taxonomies that allowed us to better characterize each task: Subject matter: 20 categories and 182 domains capturing realistic workflows and activities that can be performed in terminal. Task properties: 14 properties and 244 subproperties that describe the intent of task, initial state of the environment, applicable constraints, and deliverables types. Instruction style: 7 styles and 34 substyles representative of the ways in which users typically interact with terminal agents. All tasks were labeled against the taxonomies, providing up to 460 tags per task. Shown in Figure 19 is an example of the task intent across the environments used in training. Each task may have multiple intents to better represent complex multi-step workflows. Together with embedding-based similarity checks, these tags allowed us to filter out near-duplicates or templated tasks, and ensured that each task seen in training covered distinct aspect seen in real terminal workflows. Quality. All of our tasks went through multiple filtering stages to ensure that only the highest-quality tasks were retained for training. These stages focused on flagging and removing tasks that could be detrimental for RL, such as those with flawed environments that made the goal unachievable, noisy or misaligned verifiers, and tasks that exposed privileged information allowing agents to bypass the intended work. Rule-Based Checks. Upfront rule-based methods were used to check for basic compatibility with Reflections internal sandbox infrastructure and task completeness: 1. Tasks had to be fully Harbor compatible. 2. Dockerfiles had to be well-structured to maximize layer reuse (see Section 6.6.3). 3. Any images associated with task had to be buildable. 4. An Oracle script containing the reference solution had to consistently return reward of 1.0 across 5 attempts. 5. no-op script had to consistently return reward of 0.0 across 5 attempts. 6. Checks for privileged information had to show no unintended information leakage in the agent sandbox. Quality Signals. All tasks went through comprehensive set of over 15 quality checks using an agentic judge to measure properties that rule-based methods couldnt detect. For instance, we checked for consistency between all of the requirements or constraints explicitly mentioned in the instructions, or those directly inferrable from the environment, and the behaviors tested for in the verifiers. The definitions for each of these checks were updated over time based on the following feedback: Beam Model Technical Report, Reflection Team et al. Figure 19: Intent distribution across terminal use tasks. Circles denote synthetic tasks; squares denote vendor tasks. Expert human annotators were used to measure the efficiency of the automated checks and surface misalignment between the intent of the check and the model-produced judgments. Newly discovered quality issues or systemic flaws observed in batches of vendor or synthetic tasks resulted in definitions being expanded. For instance, we found that subset of synthetic tasks required the agent to interact with black-box binaries that the agent was freely able to access and reverse-engineer. By continuously monitoring task quality, and the reliability of our automated quality checks, we were able to make targeted improvements to synthetic pipelines and work with vendors to improve upstream task quality. Difficulty and Robustness Solvability. Static checks through oracle scripts are necessary but not sufficient to assess the health of task: the oracle scripts do not always exercise the solution paths that an agent may find, and they can obfuscate fundamental issues with the agent environment. We therefore validated tasks through end-to-end rollouts with live agents. We discarded tasks that strong model failed to solve within 𝑘 attempts. Although repeated failure does not prove that task is ill-specified or impossible, it provided practical filtering criterion. For successful rollouts, we used judge to check for reward hacking and environment issues, such as missing tools, that may have interfered with the intended solution. Adversarial Robustness. We also performed substantial filtering of reward-hackable tasks. To do so, we built an adversarial agent that actively attempted to obtain reward of 1.0 with an insufficient or incorrect solution. The agent was provided with full taxonomy of reward hacks and instructed to test out different approaches to fully assess the robustness of the verifiers. We filtered out all tasks that were hacked by this agent. 38 Beam Model Technical Report, Reflection Team et al. Figure 20: Synthetic pipeline for terminal. Verifier Robustness. Verifiers are central to RL: they evaluate an agents work and produce the reward used for training. Their quality directly shapes the training signal. For terminal tasks, verifiers were typically custom shell or Python scripts that check an agents solution (e.g., inspecting files, validating computed values, or measuring runtime). Good verifiers have three essential properties: alignment with the task description, comprehensive coverage, and robustness to reward hacking. Alignment with the Task Description. The tasks state requirements needed to be enforced without imposing unstated constraints or assuming particular implementation. As an example, if the task left the deliverables file format unspecified the verifier had to be capable of checking range of reasonable formats, rather than arbitrarily allow for single format. Comprehensive Coverage. Each individual constraint or requirement required by the task had to be tested for by the verifier. If task asked the agent to compute results across range of inputs, the verifier had to validate all those inputs thoroughly. Incomplete checks could reward partial solutions, reinforcing behavior that fell short of the tasks requirements. Robustness to Reward Hacking. verifier should reward successful task completion and resist attempts to manipulate the evaluation. For example, test inputs and expected outputs should be protected from agent modification; otherwise, an agent may change the test data to make an incorrect solution pass. Each task consisted of question and gold or ground-truth answer. Of these, many were filtered for being too easy or for having quality issues. In the final pool we had 65% math questions, 17% physics, 11% chemistry, 4% biology, and the rest from other scientific disciplines. Verification To grade the models answers to math and science questions, we instructed the model to output its final answer within boxed{} and used that syntax to extract the answer from the models response. We restricted math questions to those with numeric or symbolic answer which could be compared to the models answer using SymPy-based verification [69]. Science questions were graded using judge verifier which was prompted to compare the gold answer with the models answer, given the question. Challenges with Verification. For verification of math questions, we started from an implementation based on the math-verify library [70]. We noticed that the original implementation lacked several crucial normalizations: (a) limited support for stylistic commands, (b) no support for European style interval markers, (c) ASCII style answers (sqrt(13) instead of sqrt{13}), etc. We added support for these additional normalizations, reducing the false negative rate in verification. We also noticed that the original implementation was prone to false positives, due to incorrect SymPy object resolution. We resolved this by routing the answer to the appropriate SymPy object resolution classLaTeX for symbolic answers, and Expr for numeric answers. In addition to these, we filtered questions if the verification function could not resolve SymPy object for the gold answer. This avoided situations where the ultimate verification degenerated to string match, highly false negative prone mechanism. We found that some questions under-specified the form of the answer, making it difficult to grade. For example, if the gold answer is 3.5 m/s, we found that judge verifiers were often inconsistent in accepting more precise answers (e.g. 3.51 m/s) or those in different units (351 cm/s). Similarly, some questions required the use of wellknown constants to calculate the answer, but the model can end up with different answersand receive different rewardsdepending on the precision chosen for those constants (e.g. 9.8 m/s2 vs 9.81 m/s2 for gravitational acceleration). Because of these inconsistencies, the model may be sometimes rewarded and sometimes penalized for what is otherwise correct reasoning. To avoid this issue of noisy rewards, we rewrote questions to specify the precision, units, and any relevant constants needed. This ensured that if the model followed correct reasoning it always ended up at the gold answer. Quality Filters We applied extensive quality filters both to the question and to the answer. Strong-vs-Weak Gap. Following Cheng et al. [71], we filtered out questions where strong model performed worse than weak model, as these questions are more likely to have incorrect gold answers. It also served the purpose of informing whether or not deeper reasoning abilities are needed to solve problem. Guessability. Questions where the answers are guessable pose serious problem to the model. These questions can cause the model to learn taking guess at the answer in its chain of thought, rather than arriving at it through sound derivation. Such behavior hinders the scaling of chain of thought tokens, as the model degenerates to guess-based policy. Thus, we filtered out questions whose answer could be guessed without doing the work, such as yes/no or multiple choice; whose wording hands the reader short list of candidate answers; where what is asked (such as rank of matrix, or finite outcome probability mass questions) leaves only few possible answers; whose reference answer is unusually frequent across the full task pool (such as 0, 1, 𝜋, etc.); which are answerable by reciting memorized definition or formula; and which accidentally reveal or trivialize the answer. Broken Questions. On the other end of the difficulty spectrum, we found many questions to be broken. Similarly to guessable questions, broken questions can introduce noise into the rewards if the model can sometimes get the answer right by assuming things unstated in the question. Thus, we filtered out questions which refer to figure, table, earlier sub-question, or passage that is not included; which are self-contradictory, missing an assumption, or open to more than one reading; or which otherwise leave out information needed to pin down single answer. 41 Beam Model Technical Report, Reflection Team et al. Broken Answers. The gold answers may themselves be incorrect. We leveraged several strategies to detect wrong answers, including: asking model to review the gold answer and judge it as correct or incorrect; asking model to re-derive the gold answer with tools; and asking several independent solvers to re-derive the gold answer and only accepting the question if they agreed. Question Format. We also filtered out questions whose text requested format contradicting the standard training format (boxed{}); which contained spurious characters or formatting defects; and those in non-English languages. Verification Limitations. As described above, we restricted ourselves to short answers which could be graded by SymPy or simple judge. To meet this requirement, we filtered questions asking for several separate answers at once (which cannot be checked as one right-or-wrong result) and those asking for proof or written explanation (which require more sophisticated judge or rubric-based verification). We limited the length of model-generated answers to 200 characters (or, for the small fraction of tasks having long gold answers, 3 the number of characters of the gold answer) to avoid hedging or other forms of reward hacking. We also found that some symbolic answers could not be parsed correctly by SymPy, and filtered these out. Finally, there were questions which could not be reliably graded by the judge (e.g., the judge would sometimes give different rewards to the same answer), and we filtered these out as well. Easy Filtering. Questions that are very easy for the model can cause wasted inference compute during RL training, failing to provide non-zero gradients. To this end, we also filtered out questions which the initial checkpoint could solve frequently, with low thinking budget. Synthetic Pipelines Science Q&A Platform. Online science forums such as the Physics, Chemistry and Biology StackExchange sites, as well as open-source science Q&A corpora, contain large volume of expert-level questions, but we found that few of them are directly usable for RL: forum posts have no reference answer, questions often ask for an explanation or derivation rather than value, and many depend on context from the surrounding thread. We built pipeline that turns this seed material into verifiable short-answer tasks. The pipeline starts by extracting question-answer pairs. model rewrites each forum post into one or more self-contained questions, turning requests for proof, derivation or explanation into questions with short, checkable answer (e.g. derive the moment of inertia of uniform disk becomes what is the moment of inertia of uniform disk of mass and radius R?). It then synthesizes concise answer from the replies and extracts short reference answer (a number with units, formula, name, or short phrase) grounded in the replies. The remaining steps aim to make each question reliably gradable. Even when the reference answer is correct, grading is inconsistent whenever the question leaves room for equally correct answers: different units or precision, an unstated sign convention, or synonym for phrase answer. model therefore reviews each question against its reference answer, and rewrites the question so that the reference becomes the unique correct answer, without changing what is asked or hinting at the value, or flags it as unrepairable. The rewritten question is then solved several times by model, each attempt is graded by the same judge used in training, and final diagnosis step reviews the question, the reference, and the graded attempts together. It distinguishes wrong references (several attempts agree against the reference), ambiguous questions (rejected attempts that are defensible under another reading) and judge noise (equivalent answers graded differently) from genuine difficulty. Each task paired problem statement with test suite and comparison script, and asked the model to produce runnable solution. Quantity. We ingested and assessed problems both from open-source corpora [72, 73] and licensed from online coding platforms. Language. All the prompts of the tasks are language agnostic: they ask for code that receives inputs via stdin and emits outputs via stdout, and the test cases are simply files of inputs and expected outputs. This means that these tasks can theoretically be used to train the model in any language that supports stdin and stdout. However, the test cases and timeouts are often calibrated for specific language; specifically, test cases calibrated for higher performance languages (such as C++) may become impossible for programs written in lower performance languages (such as Python). In these cases, we generated reference solutions in Python and excluded the task from Python candidacy if the reference solution runtime was out-of-distribution. The final languages we chose to use for these tasks were Python and C++. The choice of which language task was to use was randomly selected at runtime. All tasks were eligible to be completed in C++, and 70% of these were also eligible to be completed in Python. In similar manner, we mixed in the ability for the model to use bash tool, so the model learned both to write logically and syntactically correct problems without relying on code execution, as well as test its code when possible. 43 Beam Model Technical Report, Reflection Team et al. Each task consisted of question, gold answer, and web search tools which accessed the internet via third-party search provider. Tasks Sourcing. We began by sourcing web search tasks from open-source corpora, vendors, and synthetic pipeline based on InfoSeek [74]. The open-source tasks came from OpenSeeker [75], whose questions are similar to InfoSeeks but obfuscated with multiple constraints per answer, and from DeepDive [76], mix of questions based on Wikipedia (and other knowledge-graph sources) and academic publications. Our tasks covered broad range of topics, including history, art, finance, sports, science & technology, media, law, and more. Tools. All search environments exposed two tools to the model: search tool and browse tool. The search tool accepts query string and returns URLs along with page titles and snippets that preview relevant page content, with content averaging around 200 characters per snippet. The browse tool accepts URL and returns the page rendered as Markdown, capped at 8K tokens. It also supports arguments from the command-line tool ripgrep [77]. When supplied, these arguments are applied to the full Markdown representation, allowing the model to search within the page and retrieve targeted excerpts. Verification. We used regular expression to extract the excerpt of the agents final message starting with The answer is: and ending at newline or citation. We assigned rewards based on this excerpt using three-stage procedure: 1. Exact Match: We normalized the proposed and reference answers and compared them. An exact match received reward of one. Answers that could not be extracted received reward of zero. 2. Length Check: If the answers did not match, we assigned reward of zero when the proposed answer exceeded max(150, len(gold_answer) * 4.5). This discouraged increasingly verbose answers that hedged or offered multiple alternatives. 3. Model-Based Judgment: Answers that passed the length check were evaluated by judge for equivalence to the reference answer. The judging prompt included few-shot examples illustrating how to handle ambiguity and reject hedged answers. Quality and Difficulty Filtering We excluded questions that met any of the following criteria: Answer Leakage. We dropped questions containing answer-revealing text, as determined by lexical string comparison and judge-based checks. We also examined URLs searched by the model, and implemented blocklists to target URLs which exposed the question/answer pair. We used two-layered approach: (1) explicitly flagging URL patterns corresponding to known answer dumps, including datasets, papers, and blogs; (2) dynamic blocklist that fuzzy matched both question and answer in page. Memorization. We dropped questions which could be answered by model without access to search tools, indicating questions whose answers likely appear frequently on the internet and may be memorized. Solvability. We dropped questions whose solution paths relied on websites which our search tool could not access. For example, not all search engines use the same index, and some questions required pages that were not present in the index of our search provider. Some pages were also inaccessible despite being indexed; e.g. gated behind CAPTCHA. 45 Beam Model Technical Report, Reflection Team et al. Incorrect Gold Answers. We also dropped questions for which model, given both the question and gold answer, judged the answer invalid. Similarly, we also filtered questions where model preferred common alternative answer over the gold answer, where it judged the question contradictory (because neither answer satisfied its constraints), or where it judged the question underspecified (because both answers satisfied its constraints). We identified common alternative answers by sampling multiple rollouts per question and extracting answers that occurred multiple times. Unreliable Grading. Sometimes, the judges graded equivalent answers differently, accepted substantively different answers as correct, or exhibited subjectivity in its judgments. We dropped any question that triggered this inconsistent behavior in the judge. Language. We excluded questions whose primary language was not English, as determined by language-model classifier. Difficulty Filtering. We retained tasks for which strong models solve rate exceeded weak models by at least 12.5 percentage points, or the weak models solve rate was zero. This was to ensure that all questions contained reward signal; questions for which weak model outperforms strong model often indicate problem such as an incorrect but plausible answer. Synthetic Pipeline In addition to open-source and vendor tasks, we experimented with synthetic task generation following InfoSeek [74], in which planner agent and browser agent build question backwards from single Wikipedia answer entity, adding hops and constraints until the answer is uniquely identified. The main differences between our pipeline and the original InfoSeek pipeline were: 1. Our pipeline truncated each article to 20K tokens, instead of the original 1K. 2. We required answers to have Wikipedia page exceeding 200 words. 3. We implemented retries for validation failures. 4. We further filtered questions through multi-stage grading funnel. This grading funnel included all the quality and difficulty filters described in the previous section, plus two additional filters. First, we also asked another model to validate whether the question was valid given the claims from the parent/children trees built during the synthesis pipeline. Second, given the source pages built during the synthesis pipeline, we asked another model to judge whether the answer was grounded in the supporting evidence. Although we found tasks generated by the InfoSeek pipeline to be useful earlier in our development cycle, we found that by the end of Beams training they were largely too easy. 4.1.10 Professional Knowledge Work Beyond terminal and software-engineering tasks, we trained Beam on broader class of professional work. Frontier agents need to do more than write code: they need to understand source material, use the right tools, and produce the artifacts that real organizations rely on, including reports, spreadsheets, presentations, and other business documents. Our real-world corporate tasks were built around this idea: we put the agent in realistic professional setting and asked it to deliver the kind of finished work one would expect from someone in that job (Figure 24). When producing artifacts like reports or presentations, there is usually no simple unit test to check whether the output is right: it has to make sense, be consistent, be backed up by evidence, and be useful in practice. The central technical challenge was therefore how to evaluate and reward this kind of work. Since we could not run test suite and get pass or fail, we used an agentic judge to inspect the final deliverables and decide whether they were high-quality and correct. This changed how we approached task design, reward construction, and defense against reward hacking compared to classic software engineering. Sourcing We began with broad pool of tasks covering wide range of occupations and industry sectors, with an emphasis on realistic artifact-producing professional work. Tasks came from both our synthetic generation pipeline and external vendors, and were filtered through our quality, difficulty, and integrity checks. 46 Beam Model Technical Report, Reflection Team et al. Figure 24: Agentic knowledge-work environments and task curation. The largest sectors in the final pool were finance & insurance, health care & social assistance, and professional, scientific & technical services. Required deliverables included .docx, .xlsx, .md, .csv, .pdf, and .pptx, alongside other formats. Many tasks required multiple output formats, and tasks were evaluated against weighted rubric criteria, including penalty criteria for undesirable outputs. Every task was authored as Harbor task directory and ships as digest-pinned container image built from its environment, together with its source assets. Synthetic Task Generation Synthetic Pipeline. Our synthetic knowledge-work tasks were produced by the same three-stage recipe as our terminal tasks (Figure 20), re-grounded in professional work. Seeds were real professional documents drawn from curated web corpus, each paired with an occupation sampled from the pre-defined skill set and taxonomy (sector, then occupation group, then O*NET code). An authoring agent working in Docker-enabled sandbox then built the complete task folder in one episode: manager-voice instruction, two to five reference documents with the seed preserved byte-for-byte, golden deliverables, the weighted rubric, and the environment image. As with terminal tasks, every submission had to clear quality gate of static checks plus tool-using judge: eight deterministic validators and nine judged criteria spanning professional meaningfulness, difficulty, rubric coverage, and ground-truth protection. Per-criterion feedback was returned to the authoring agent for up to ten revision rounds. Because authoring and in-loop judging shared model family, accepted tasks additionally passed an independent majority-vote quality filter from different model family (three votes over five defect classes, retaining roughly 42% of published tasks), before the solvability screening. Environment Design. Each task was packaged in Harbor format as reproducible workspace containing the task instructions, source artifacts, and the tools and applications needed for execution, so the agent operated in controlled environment that could be reproduced consistently across validation and training. Agent execution took place in an untrusted sandbox, while grading was performed separately in trusted evaluation sandbox by tool-using judge that inspected generated files, verified calculations and sources, and applied the task-specific rubric. Verification. We designed both the task and how we evaluated it at the same time. Rubrics were authored alongside each task by decomposing the intended professional deliverable into atomic, independently verifiable criteria spanning content, structure, functionality, and presentation. We calibrated their coverage and granularity so that distinct facts, calculations, comparisons, recommendations, and failure modes could be scored separately, while weighting each criterion according to its professional consequence rather than simply its level of detail. Rubrics were then further refined through downstream quality checks and adversarial analysis (especially whitebox attacking): grader failures, reward-hacking traces, and model rollouts were used to identify criteria that were underspecified, overly coarse, redundant, or vulnerable to shortcuts, and to improve both the rubric and grader before training. 47 Beam Model Technical Report, Reflection Team et al. tool-using judge evaluated each submitted artifact against the resulting rubric by inspecting files, checking calculations and source material, and scoring each criterion independently. We then aggregated these criterionlevel judgments and applied threshold selected through extensive experiments for training stability and learning effectiveness; submissions that met the threshold received binary reward of 1, while those that did not received 0. Quality Control Tasks passed through staged and heuristic-based quality-control and derisking funnel before entering training. Static Checks. We first applied rubric-level quality checks for coverage, atomicity, observability, non-duplication, and appropriate weighting. Adversarial Probes. Next, we adversarially probed the surviving tasks using both white-box and black-box attackers. White-box attackers were given the task together with its rubric and grading specification, allowing them to directly probe weaknesses in rubric design and identify ways to earn credit without achieving the intended goal. Black-box attackers saw only the solver-facing task and environment, and were used primarily to test the intrinsic quality of the task itself, including ambiguity, missing information, unintended shortcuts, and other specification gaps. Separate rubric and goal judges then evaluated the same frozen deliverables: the rubric judge checked whether the stated criteria were satisfied, while the goal judge independently checked whether the artifact actually achieved the underlying professional objective. Disagreement between the two exposed potentially underspecified or exploitable tasks. Solvability. Candidate tasks were subsequently validated through model rollouts to establish empirical solvability, followed by RL derisking runs under the same reward setup used for training. Failures discovered at later stages fed back into the earlier quality-control process: problematic tasks were revised or removed, while rubric criteria and grader checks were updated to close the observed gaps before the task was re-evaluated. Reward Integrity. Letting judge assign rewards introduces its own failure modes. An agent may produce outputs that superficially satisfy the rubric without completing the intended work, exploit weaknesses in how evidence is judged, or attempt to influence the evaluator through the artifact or environment. Reward integrity therefore depends on the model, task environment, and evaluatornot just the scoring prompt. We addressed this by auditing both the final deliverable and the trajectory used to produce it. During training, an online integrity judge checked whether the policy earned, or attempted to earn, rubric credit through shortcuts such as unsupported provenance, surface-level criterion gaming, or evaluator manipulation; detected cases received zero reward. Offline audits then inspected artifacts and trajectories for new or ambiguous failure modes and fed those findings back into the task, rubric, and online judge. Tasks with credible shortcuts or evaluator exploits were removed from subsequent training mixtures until they were repaired and revalidated. 4.1.11 General Tool Use To teach the model to perform general tool use, we sourced singleand multi-turn tasks requiring the model to call diverse set of tools. Tasks were graded via programmatic rules and/or rubrics. In all cases, score of one was assigned only when the task passed all scoring criteria; there was no partial credit. Meta Tools. tasks tools were presented in one of two ways. The alignment teachers starting point was the same midtrained checkpoint used for its sibling agentic teacher (Section 4.1), and we used similar supervised fine-tuning (SFT) and reinforcement learning (RL) recipe, with few key differences. The first difference was that steering the models behavior towards these values required broader set of SFT demonstrations and RL tasks beyond coding, STEM, and terminal use. Our data mixture spanned the domains of writing and editing, fact-finding, document understanding, open-ended conversation, and multi-turn collaboration to achieve user goals. The second difference was that model properties like helpfulness and safety cannot be easily verified programmatically. We thus used combination of verifiable checks, task-level rubrics applied by judge, and generative reward models calibrated to human ground-truth judgments. Finally, the principles we sought to teach the model were often in tension with one another. For example, safety can conflict with instruction-following, and helpfulness can come at the expense of accuracy. We took quality-over-quantity approach to constructing the data mixture and conducted shorter runs with regular human-in-the-loop evaluations. This allowed us to quickly adjust subjective criteria, tune delicate tradeoffs, catch reward hacks, and iteratively shape the models behavior. 4.2.1 Objectives We defined the desired behavior of the model in terms of hierarchy of principles [81]. The first tier of principles are invariants that the model should follow without exception, and should never be overridden by system, developer, or user messages or subsequent principles: Safety, as defined by Reflections safety guidelines. See Section 7 for details on our safety post-training. Model Identity, i.e. maintaining its core identity as an AI assistant. The second tier are commitments the model should always strive to uphold; these interact with system, developer, and user messages: Accuracy, including factuality of claims, faithfulness to the input context, and calibrated confidence about these. Instruction Following, including compliance with system and developer instructions, transparent pursuit of user objectives, and reasonable resolution of uncertainty. The third tier are helpful defaults that we want the model to maintain in the absence of other instructions. Helpfulness covers aspects of user interaction quality and style including the comprehensiveness, efficiency, proactivity, and consistency of model responses. 4.2.2 Supervised Fine-Tuning To initialize the alignment teacher, we compiled set of demonstrations spanning variety of domains and use-cases  (Table 8)  . Model Identity An influential idea in alignment research is that models learn about many different personas through pretraining, but select specific AI assistant persona through different stages of post-training [87]. It has been observed that deviations from this persona are predictive of misaligned behavior [88]; hence, we consider maintaining core identity as an AI assistant to be second invariant. In order to bake this identity into the model weights, we train the model on an RL environment that reinforces the default persona of Beam, helpful AI assistant trained by Reflection. We seeded the identity in SFT using handwritten and synthetically generated traces, half with our default system prompt and half with generic system prompt (You are helpful assistant. . . ). Our RL tasks included both realistic inquiries about model identity, as well as adversarial inquiries that attempted to alter core identity, and were scored by judge to capture nuance and negations. Accuracy & Calibrated Confidence In accordance with our model principles, we want our model to provide accurate and factual answers and be well-calibrated to the limits of its own parametric knowledge. To this end, the knowledge calibration component trains the model to only answer factual questions when it knows the answer, and to abstain when it does not. Accuracy measures whether an answer is correct, whereas calibration also asks whether the model should have answered at all. Accuracy-only training and evaluation tend to reward guessing, which helps explain why models often answer confidently when uncertain [89]. Question Generation. We generated closed-book, short-answer questions from documents in our pretraining web corpus so that correctness depends only on the models parametric knowledge. These questions are selfcontained with single answer. Additional filters removed time-sensitive questions, ambiguous questions with multiple valid answers, questions which cannot be answered using the source document, and false-premise questions. We used stratified random sampling across the six reasoning efforts and retained one filtered trace per question. Selecting RL Tasks. With abstention seeded, we selected RL tasks to maximize signal in GRPO: question teaches the model to abstain only when its responses include both abstentions and wrong answers, and to answer only when correct responses appear alongside abstentions. Rather than sampling at random, we scored 16 responses per candidate question with the RL judge and reward, discarded questions whose responses all receive the same reward (all correct, all wrong, or all abstained), and binned the rest by mean reward into five bands, drawing equally from each and requiring at least one abstention in the low-reward bands. This kept both sides of the calibration boundary represented and kept groups away from the saturated rewards at which the trainer discards them, so the components small share of the mixture stays informative throughout training. Each prompt is paired with task-specific rubrics (21.8 rubrics on average) evaluated by judge. The final reward is all-or-nothing: response receives reward 1 only if every required rubric passes. This objective produced better full-task success than either averaging the individual rubric scores or combining partial credit with an all-or-nothing term, consistent with the reward-design findings reported for AdvancedIF [96]. We extend the single-turn RL environment to instructions that evolve over conversation. Our multi-turn IF environment targets four behaviors: retaining standing instruction across turns, applying conditional instruction only when its condition is met, combining conversation-wide constraint with requirement for one turn, and replacing an earlier instruction during the conversation. Starting from filtered WildChat prompts [82], we generate constraints and conversation templates that specify when simulated user should introduce, activate, or revise an instruction. The templates include requests such as asking for clarification or requesting rewrite. The generated conversations are checked for correctness, satisfiability, and consistency between the instruction and the users underlying request. Each conversation records the constraints active on its final turn. These conversations provide disjoint SFT and RL datasets. The SFT set contains traces combining stored multiturn histories with successful final responses. The RL set contains tasks in which the policy receives stored conversation history and generates the final assistant turn. The RL reward is all-or-nothing: judge receives the active constraints and the limited context needed to evaluate them, and the response receives reward of 1 only if every active constraint is satisfied. Helpfulness In order to improve the models helpfulness and interaction quality on open-ended conversations, we trained it using an approach similar to RLHF/RLAIF [97, 98]. We treat human judgments as the ultimate source of ground-truth for the quality of conversational behavior, and collect fresh human dataper-attribute ratings and pairwise preferencesat regular cadence. We use this data to periodically calibrate proxy preference judge that we use for automated arena style evaluations, as well as generative reward model that we use in RL for on-policy evaluation. We found that with generative reward model strong enough to accurately rank rollouts and resist reward-hacking, RL in this environment steadily improves the models conversational behavior, yielding model that pushes the open Pareto frontier on our in-house arena. Human Judgment of Conversational Quality. Human judgments serve two critical roles in our training recipe. First, they define our target: both the generative reward model and the proxy judge are calibrated against human labels. Second, they are our main defense against Goodharting [99, 100]: during training, the policy can optimize rewards in ways that diverge from what humans actually prefer, and only fresh labels on the trained policys outputs can reliably detect this divergence. We collected human annotations on the overall quality of model responses, as well as specific attributes like coverage, intent understanding, clarity, tone, and focus. Our nine attributes of conversational quality are described in Table 9. Annotators rated model responses on 5-point scale on each attribute and also on pairwise preference compared to an anchor. Five annotators labeled each pair; the ground-truth label is the mean of the three most agreeing annotators. We used bank of public open-ended conversational prompts, consisting of general-knowledge and advice questions, to train our policy model via RLAIF. Comparing Models on Benchmark When comparing candidate model with baseline, we evaluated both on the same set of tasks and reported their native benchmark scores for within-benchmark comparisons, and normalized scores when combining results across benchmarks. Normalization for Aggregation For evaluations included in the cross-benchmark aggregate, we rescaled each result relative to two reference scores. If 𝑠𝑚,𝑒 is model 𝑚s raw score on evaluation 𝑒, and 𝑓𝑒 and ℎ𝑒 are its lower and upper reference scores, 𝑧𝑚,𝑒 = 𝑠𝑚,𝑒 𝑓𝑒 ℎ𝑒 𝑓𝑒 This way, the lower reference, when passed as model score, maps to zero and the upper reference to one, while values outside that range are retained rather than clipped. The lower reference represents model whose performance we aim to meet or exceed, while the upper reference represents stronger model that serves as the current target. As development progressed, we updated the upper reference with stronger models. References were held fixed for given aggregate and its confidence intervals. Because changing the references changes the normalization scale, aggregate scores are only directly comparable when computed using the same reference set. Aggregating across Benchmarks To aggregate scores across benchmarks, we started by assigning each benchmark category, such as instructionfollowing or safety. We then averaged normalized evaluation scores within categories and then averaged across categories. Formally, if 𝐸𝑐 is the set of contributing evaluations in category 𝑐, and 𝐶 is the set of contributing categories, 𝐴𝑚,𝑐 = 1 𝐸𝑐 𝑒𝐸𝑐 𝑧𝑚,𝑒, 𝑂𝑚 = 1 𝐶 𝑐𝐶 𝐴𝑚,𝑐. This gives each category equal weight and each contributing evaluation equal weight within category. We used the overall score 𝑂𝑚 as an internal summary for comparing model variants and hill-climbing target. Statistical Testing We estimated uncertainty in the overall score differences of two models using paired bootstrap over evaluation tasks. We generated 10K bootstrap replicates by resampling tasks with replacement, preserving paired model results and grouping repeated attempts within each task. For category and overall scores, we applied the same normalization and aggregation procedure within each bootstrap replicate, with reference scores held fixed. The resulting confidence intervals capture uncertainty due to the sampled evaluation tasks under the fixed evaluation setup. However, they do not capture model-training variance, systematic grading errors, or uncertainty in the normalization references. We used 2.5th and 97.5th percentiles of the resulting score differences as 95% confidence interval. Intervals excluding zero indicate statistically significant difference at the nominal 5% level. 4.3 Merging Experts with On-Policy Distillation As described in Sections 4.1 and 4.2, we train two complementary experts: an agentic expert focused on reasoning and agentic tasks, and an alignment expert focused on helpfulness, safety, and conversational behavior. We combine their capabilities into single student through multi-teacher on-policy distillation (MOPD) [64, 103106] as illustrated in Figure 30. The student generates trajectories and learns from the teachers token distributions at 60 Beam Model Technical Report, Reflection Team et al. Probabilistic Teacher Routing The student needed to retain strong reasoning capabilities while also learning the alignment teachers conversational behavior. We routed each task family to the teacher best suited to that type of data. For task families benefiting from both experts, we used mixture. OPD adds teacher annotation and full-vocabulary distillation loss to this pipeline. The main systems challenges are transporting teacher targets to the trainer and evaluating the KL without materializing full-vocabulary logit tensors for the entire batch. Transporting the Teachers Hidden States For 𝑁 token positions and vocabulary of size 𝑉, transporting full-vocabulary teacher distributions would require 𝑂(𝑁𝑉) values. We reduce communication by transporting teacher hidden states and reconstructing the logits on the trainer. This approach is also used in DeepSeek-V4 [107]. This reduces the payload to 𝑂(𝑁𝑑𝑇) values, where 𝑑𝑇 is the teachers hidden width. Token positions and teacher identities are retained through sequence packing and sharding, keeping teacher hidden states aligned with the corresponding student tokens. The trainer reconstructs each teachers logits using its cached, frozen output head and applies the teachers own logit softcap before full-vocabulary softmax normalization. The student is normalized after its own softcap, which may differ from the teachers; this preserves each models native output distribution. 61 Beam Model Technical Report, Reflection Team et al.

What Student Probabilities to Use The student that generates rollout can differ from the student being updated: while inference is running, the trainer continues to learn from other rollouts. We must therefore decide which versions disagreement with the teacher the loss should measure. We use the trainers current probabilities for both the student log probabilities and the weighting over vocabulary entries in the KL. Consider context where the current student distribution already matches the teachers. The per-token KL and its gradient are then zero, even if the earlier inference policy disagreed with the teacher. This makes each update address the disagreement that remains at update time. At each sampled context, we differentiate the full-vocabulary KL directly, summing over all next tokens using current trainer probabilities. This vocabulary sum requires no sampled-token importance correction. The contexts themselves, however, still come from the rollout-generating policy and may be stale. We treat them as fixed when differentiating the KL. Memory-Efficient Full-Vocabulary Reverse KL Computation via Blocking Transporting hidden states reduces communication, but reconstructing all teacher and student logits at once would still require 𝑂(𝑁𝑉) memory. We evaluated the same full-vocabulary reverse KL in chunks of 𝐶 token positions, reducing temporary logit memory to 𝑂(𝐶𝑉) while retaining every vocabulary entry (Figure 31). For each chunk, PyTorch [108] matrix multiplications form two 𝐶 𝑉 logit buffers in GPU memory (HBM). For simplicity, the pseudocode omits each models logit softcap, which is applied before computing the softmax normalizers and KL terms. Custom Triton [109] kernels reduce vocabulary tiles, avoiding additional chunk-wide probability and log-probability tensors. The forward pass saves the per-token KL and softmax normalizers and releases the logit buffers as shown in Algorithm 1. The backward pass follows the same chunked traversal, recomputing the logits and using the saved statistics to accumulate student gradients. This follows the same IO-aware design principles as FlashAttention [110]: tiled reductions, compact normalization statistics, and recomputation during backward. The output-head projections remain separate matrix multiplications; the 𝑂(𝐶𝑉) memory bound applies to temporary logits, with hidden states and output heads retained across forward and backward. In our system, this full-vocabulary implementation runs in roughly the same wall-clock time as our sampled-token OPD implementation. The student-sampled reverse KL estimator uses teacher log probabilities on tokens sampled from the student [105]. 4.3.3 Training Recipe and Details Our training recipe starts with SFT initialization, followed by MOPD with the teacher-routing policy and rollout settings described below. We sample new trajectories only from the student; the teachers provide token-level supervision for these trajectories. We use no external reward signal on student rollouts: the training signal comes entirely from the teachers probabilities. During MOPD, we use context length of 256K tokens. Each training step uses 𝑀 = 512 tasks with 𝑅 = 8 rollouts per task, for total of 4,096 rollouts. We use constant learning rate of 3 106 after 20 linear warm-up steps from zero. With this recipe, the merged student broadly recovers the teachers performance across the evaluated domains, as discussed in the results below. 62 Beam Model Technical Report, Reflection Team et al. We finetuned the midtrained (Section 3) checkpoint on the combined SFT data of both experts, including the alignment mixture described in Section 4.2.2. Thanks to this, the students behaviors are close to the teachers distributions from the very beginning of training. We appended to this data self-distilled traces sampled from the two experts models, which we found is important for reaching teacher-level performance downstream. Our merging recipe therefore combines offline supervised self-distillation with MOPD. In our experiments, SFT alone did not recover the performance of both experts, even with the additional expert-generated traces; we used MOPD to close the remaining gap. Teacher Routing For instruction following, grounded queries, and long-context tasks, 5050 mixture gives each expert an equal probability of supervising rollout. We decided to supervise General Tool Use by both experts because workflow automation needs both the strong reasoning capability of the agentic teacher to coordinate actions across many tools and the alignment teachers complex instruction following and preference alignment. Table 10 summarizes the routing policy. Nucleus Sampling for the Student Consistent with the RL run, we applied nucleus sampling (𝑝 = 0.99) when generating student rollouts to reduce problematic sequences caused by sampling low-probability tokens. On the trainer, we evaluated Equation (4.1) over the full vocabulary for both student and teacher. We did not mask or renormalize either distribution to the rollout nucleus, because doing so would change the distributions being matched, including the teachers target. Truncating the teacher to its own nucleus could also assign zero probability to tokens with nonzero student probability, making the reverse KL infinite. 63 Beam Model Technical Report, Reflection Team et al. With sampled-token KL, the same rollout samples determine both the visited contexts and the Monte Carlo estimate of KL within each context. Under nucleus sampling, tokens outside the nucleus cannot enter that estimate and receive no direct comparison with the teacher at that context. Our full-vocabulary loss includes those tokens at every visited context, keeping rollout truncation separate from the vocabulary sum. 4.3.4 Results on Merged Model In Table 11, we compare the merged student with the two teachers. The student broadly recovers their performance across the evaluated domains: it is competitive with the agentic teacher on agentic coding and mathematics and science benchmarks, matches or exceeds the alignment teacher on the lanes it supervises, and exceeds the stronger teacher where both supervise lane. The merged model carries both teachers capabilities, with some remaining performance gaps. The broader model comparisons in Section 5 use temperature 0.7; this teacherstudent comparison uses 1.0. Safety transfer is analyzed in Section 7.2.3. Split Braining Multi-teacher distillation can exhibit incomplete capability transfer and interactions across domains, even when each domain is assigned its own teacher. These integration challenges motivate us to test distinct potential failure mode: whether the merged student retains teacher-associated behaviors that depend on prompt-distribution cues, rather than reliably combining the teachers capabilities. We refer to this behavior as split-braining. To test for this behavior, we developed suite of hybrid tasks that combine features of both teachers prompt distributions, embedding challenging reasoning problems within conversational prompts. On these hybrid tasks, we did not observe significant degradation in performance, suggesting that reasoning performance is maintained even in alignment contexts. However, in constructing these hybrid tasks, we found that models sometimes ignored small modifications to the prompt, such as changing the requested output format, and required stronger distributional cues to elicit alignment-associated behavior. This suggests that certain features associated with the agentic teachers prompt distribution are relatively deeply ingrained. Encouragingly, reasoning performance remained intact even when stronger alignment-associated cues were introduced. 4.4 RL Infrastructure The post-training stages described above require infrastructure that can support long-horizon agent interactions alongside continual model updates. The central challenge is to sustain high throughput while managing policy staleness, adapting to changing workloads, and recovering from failures. We built an asynchronous RL stack that separates training, inference, and tool execution, allowing resources to be allocated according to their distinct demands. The architecture also separates the learning recipe from execution infrastructure, enabling rapid experimentation throughout the training campaign. Across twelve production jobs, the system processed more than 80M rollout executions, with configured capacity reaching 1,920 trainer GPUs and 8,576 inference GPUs. The broader post-training campaign, including derisking 64 Beam Model Technical Report, Reflection Team et al.
