Below, we describe the architecture and key design choices that supported this scale, followed by lessons from production experience. 4.4.1 Architecture Overview The architecture separates the RL recipe from distributed execution through stable interfaces for rollout generation, sampling, and preparation of training samples. These interfaces allow researchers to control which tasks run and how their results contribute to learning, while the infrastructure handles placement, scheduling, data movement, and recovery. Figure 32 shows the main components and their interactions. The control service manages the job lifecycle and coordinates rollout generation, batch assembly, and policy updates. Rollout workers execute agentenvironment interactions using policy inference and sandboxes for tool execution, with separate judge model reviewing solutions where enabled. The training service consumes completed batches and updates the policy, while the control service coordinates the publication and adoption of new policy versions. Storage preserves checkpoints and execution records. Each job runs in dedicated Ray cluster [113] with topology-aware placement and concurrent initialization of training and inference services. Generation begins once the data-pipeline state and initial policy weights have been initialized or restored. During training, the control service exchanges metadata and references, while trainer nodes fetch their assigned batch data and serving instances pull and verify updated weights directly from trainer memory. Keeping bulk transfers off the coordination path allows data movement to scale with the training and inference fleets. Rollout workers and serving instances can recover locally from isolated failures. Failures of the trainer or control service instead trigger coordinated restart from completed checkpoint, restoring the model, optimizer, and corresponding data-pipeline state. 65 Beam Model Technical Report, Reflection Team et al. Figure 32: High-level architecture of the asynchronous RL stack. The control service coordinates rollout generation, batch preparation, and policy updates. Rollout workers interact with policy inference, sandbox, and optional judge services. The training service consumes completed rollout data and publishes updated policy weights, while storage preserves checkpoints and execution records. Arrows show logical interactions rather than transport protocols. Control Service The control service coordinates rollout generation, batch preparation, and policy updates as concurrent activities. Rollout workers generate trajectories and evaluate task outcomes, completed samples are assembled into training batches according to the learning recipe, and updated policy weights are made available to inference workers. This organization allows generation and optimization to overlap despite substantial variation in rollout duration. Rollout admission limits and bounded buffering regulate the flow of work through the system. When training consumption slows, these controls reduce further admission rather than allowing completed samples to accumulate indefinitely. Their settings balance keeping the trainer supplied against limiting policy staleness. They do not impose hard bound on token age, since long-running trajectories can span multiple policy updates. Inference workers adopt updated weights asynchronously, verifying each update before resuming generation. Different workers may therefore serve different policy versions, and single trajectory may span several versions. We retain per-token policy-version records through batch preparation to support staleness monitoring and diagnosis of training behavior. Policy Inference Service Serving Mesh. The policy inference service is built on SGLang [114]. Each serving instance distributes inference across multiple GPUs, with attention computation and KV caches assigned to individual ranks and expert computation distributed across the instance. This organization supports concurrent generation for many long-running agent trajectories. 66 Beam Model Technical Report, Reflection Team et al. Figure 33: Policy updates during multi-turn rollout. Within policy version, subsequent turns reuse cached context and prefill only newly added tokens. When weights change during decoding, the running turn retains its existing KV cache. At the next turn, the full context is recomputed under the updated weights using previously recorded expert selections. Widths are schematic. Weight Updates and Prefill Expert Replay. Long rollouts can span multiple policy updates (Figure 33). In-flight requests retain their KV caches when adopting new weights, allowing generation to continue without restarting the trajectory. At the next turn following weight update, earlier context is recomputed under the current weights, replaying the expert selections recorded during prior generation. Request placement preserves cache locality across turns. This approach allows ongoing rollouts to incorporate policy updates, but means that decoding within turn can combine updated weights with cached attention state computed under earlier weights. Policy-version records accompany generated tokens through training, supporting the staleness diagnostics discussed in Section 4.4.2. Prefill Scheduling. Long, multi-turn trajectories require substantial input processing alongside ongoing decoding, including recomputation of earlier context after policy updates. Because attention ranks share expert-parallel resources, prefill work on one rank can delay decoding on others. We coordinate prefills across ranks to reduce interference between input processing and token generation. Grouping prefills into waves leaves intervening decode steps free to use low-latency DeepEP [115] dispatch. We also limit concurrent inference requests to preserve memory for KV caches. Together with the admission controls described in Section 4.4.1, these mechanisms regulate resource use as rollout lengths and task mixtures change. Training Service The training service consumes asynchronously generated rollouts and produces policy updates. It must accommodate substantial variation in sequence length while preserving the sampling records and sample weights required by the learning recipe. Batch preparation overlaps optimization, and updated weights are published to the inference service as training progresses. Distributed Training and Batch Preparation. We use Megatron-style distributed training [41], combining tensor, expert, and data parallelism with activation recomputation to support long-context optimization. Rollouts are packed by length to reduce padding and distributed across training replicas to limit workload imbalance. Packing preserves sequence boundaries, prevents attention across independent sequences, and keeps token-level metadata aligned with the corresponding samples. Sample weights are preserved through batch preparation so that changes in packing or placement do not alter their contributions to the training objective. Sampling Consistency and Memory Efficiency. The trainer supports the sampling and routing consistency measures described in Section 4.1.2. Recorded expert selections are reused during training, while activations and routing scores are recomputed under the current weights. Token probabilities are normalized over the nuclei recorded during generation. To reduce memory demand for long sequences, we compute the required token probabilities without materializing the full vocabulary-logit tensor. Together with activation recomputation and sequence packing, this limits the memory overhead of training on long agentic trajectories. 67 Beam Model Technical Report, Reflection Team et al. Figure 34: Overlap between rollout generation, batch preparation, and training. The next batch is prepared while the trainer processes the current batch, and updated policy weights become available as training progresses. Inference workers adopt updates asynchronously. The one-batch lookahead is illustrative and does not bound policy age to one version. Widths are schematic. Weight Distribution. Frequent policy updates must be transferred from the trainer to inference workers that may use different sharding layout. We transfer weights directly from trainer memory using NIXL [116], avoiding the need to write and reload durable checkpoint for each update. The transfer process accommodates the different layouts, and serving instances verify received weights before adopting them. This allows policy publication and inference updates to proceed without synchronizing the entire serving fleet. Checkpointing and Recovery. Because rollout generation and batch preparation can advance ahead of optimization, recovery requires consistent record of both training and data-pipeline progress. Checkpoints therefore capture the model, optimizer, training counters, and corresponding data-pipeline state. Following trainer or coordination failure, the job restores completed checkpoint and loads the restored policy into the inference service before generation resumes. Work beyond the checkpoint boundary may be discarded and regenerated. This provides consistent recovery point without requiring exact replay of previously generated rollouts or prepared batches. Shared Infrastructure Services Sandbox execution, judging, and data preparation sit outside the core RL stack and are managed as part of the broader infrastructure effort. Sandbox Service. Tool-using rollouts execute commands in sandboxes created from task-specific Open Container Initiative (OCI) images. Each sandbox preserves its own files and processes across turns. Tool results and structured failure details return to the rollout actor; the rollout environment defines task behavior and rewards. The sandbox fleet scaled independently of training and inference. Judge Service. Where enabled, separately served, fixed judge model reviews rollouts that passed automated task checks against versioned assessment criteria and can veto pass before reward reaches training. Its endpoint scales independently and does not participate in policy weight updates. Under fail-closed configuration, judge request that still fails after retries fails the rollout, preventing an unreviewed verifier pass from becoming positive training reward (see Section 6). Data Preparation. The data pipeline assembles task mixtures and associates each task with its environment, tools, and scoring rules. Its progress is saved alongside training checkpoints so that resumed jobs remain consistent with the restored training state (see Section 6). 68 Beam Model Technical Report, Reflection Team et al. Figure 35: Sources of policy staleness across production jobs. The stacked components measure policy-version differences within rollouts, between rollouts in group, between groups for task, and the remaining gap at training consumption. Differences between rollouts in the same group were the largest component. All components share common normalization: the mean total policy age over valid measurement windows is set to 1. The horizontal axis concatenates recorded 30-minute windows across twelve jobs, omitting gaps between jobs; alternating shaded bands distinguish jobs. The breakdown was recorded for eleven jobs, with unavailable measurements left blank. Policy age measures version differences, not elapsed time. 4.4.2 Production Experience Operating the RL stack across twelve production jobs highlighted the interaction between workload characteristics, policy staleness, and resource utilization. As task mixtures and rollout lengths changed, maintaining efficient training required monitoring the full path from generation to optimization. We summarize four operational lessons below. Balancing Throughput and Policy Freshness. The concurrency needed to keep the trainer supplied varied with rollout duration and task mix. We increased rollout admission when insufficient batch supply left the trainer waiting, and reduced it when generation outpaced consumption or policy age increased. In pre-run tuning sweep, increasing concurrency beyond serving capacity added latency without improving generation throughput. Effective concurrency therefore depended on the workload and had to be revisited throughout training. Understanding Policy Staleness. Per-token policy-version records allowed us to distinguish staleness accumulated within individual trajectories, differences between related rollouts, and the remaining gap before training consumed the data (see Figure 35). Across the instrumented runs, version differences between rollouts in the same group were the largest component of policy age. This showed that managing staleness required attention to uneven trajectory progress as well as queueing. Combined with execution traces and queue metrics, these measurements informed adjustments to rollout admission and helped diagnose delays in the training pipeline. Model Behavior and Memory Demand. Sequence length alone did not determine training memory requirements. We observed cases in which generated content concentrated token assignments on small subset of MoE experts, causing out-of-memory failures despite remaining within the configured sequence-length limits. Some incidents involved repetitive outputs; another followed task-mixture change without repetition. These failures showed that token counts and aggregate memory metrics were insufficient to characterize memory pressure: monitoring expert-routing concentration was also important. Input Processing in Long-Horizon Rollouts. High cache reuse did not eliminate substantial prefill work. Multi-turn trajectories repeatedly submitted growing conversation histories, and fresh input-token volume remained larger than generated-token volume through much of the run, despite cache-hit rates above 94%. Cache-hit percentage alone therefore understated the input-processing workload. These observations reinforced the impor69 Beam Model Technical Report, Reflection Team et al. tance of measuring fresh prefill separately from decoding and coordinating the two workloads, as described above. The token-volume measurements do not directly measure their relative compute costs. 4.5 Quantization Beam is available in BF16, FP8, and NVFP4 precision formats. The two quantized checkpoints are produced from the same BF16 model using post-training quantization (PTQ), without further model training. They offer different trade-offs in model footprint, supported hardware, and serving efficiency while retaining much of the BF16 models evaluated capability. Quantization Scheme FP8 stores weights and input activations as 8-bit E4M3 numbers. Weights have fixed scale per output channel; activation scales are computed dynamically per token during inference. FP8 conversion is applied to the following components: Attention blocks (query, key, value, output, and attention projections), dense MLPs, MoE experts block (gate, up, and down projections), and KV Cache. Embeddings, the language modeling head, MoE routers, and normalization layers retain their original precision and values. Quantization Method We used post-training quantization (PTQ) to convert selected BF16 weights to FP8 using the round-to-nearest (RTN) method. This requires no additional training or calibration dataset. At given quantized layer, let 𝑣𝑟,𝑗 denote either weight or an input activation, with 𝑟 indexing output channels for weights or tokens for activations and 𝑗 indexing input features. For nonzero vector, both cases use the same scale and rounding rule: 𝑠𝑟 = max𝑗 𝑣𝑟,𝑗 448 , 𝑞𝑟,𝑗 = roundE4M3 ( 𝑣𝑟,𝑗 𝑠𝑟 ) . The quantized values represent 𝑣𝑟,𝑗 𝑠𝑟𝑞𝑟,𝑗. Weight scales are computed separately for each output channel during conversion and remain fixed during inference. Activation scales are recomputed from the current inputs for each token at each quantized layer on every forward pass, so no offline activation calibration is required. Here, 448 is the largest finite FP8 E4M3 value, and roundE4M3 rounds to the nearest representable value. All-zero channels or activation vectors use positive fallback scale to avoid division by zero [118]. 70 Beam Model Technical Report, Reflection Team et al. 4.5.2 NVFP The NVFP4 checkpoint was quantized using NVIDIAs Model Optimizer [119], built and maintained by the NVIDIA team. Quantization Scheme NVFP4 stores values as 4-bit E2M1 numbers with one FP8 (E4M3) scale per 16-element block and one FP32 scale per tensor. In the NVFP4 release, MoE experts use NVFP4 W4A4 precision, while dense MLPs, attention, embeddings, and the LM head remain in BF16. The MoE router remains in FP32. The KV cache remains in BF16, with FP8 supported. Quantization Method For each 16-element weight block, we picked the FP8 scale that minimizes output error using Model Optimizers Local Hessian algorithm [120]. We start from the BF16 checkpoint and calibrate one decoder layer at time across 8 GPUs. Every layer sees the BF16 models activations, not those of already-quantized layers, and statistics are reduced across ranks before the search so every rank selects identical scales. Our calibration set is composed of 1,000 long agentic trajectories of 32,768 tokens each (32.8M tokens), mostly software-engineering sessions, rendered in Beams chat format. Beam serves long-horizon agentic work, so we calibrate on sequences of the same kind. The calibration took around 6 hours on one node of 8 B300 GPUs and used under 30 GiB of GPU memory per rank. We tried different NVFP4 quantization recipes on the BF16 checkpoint with the same data, seed and pipeline. Our primary metric is held-out fidelity to BF16 in terms of KL(BF16NVFP4) and top-1 agreement, measured teacher-forced on 64 agentic sequences of 32,768 tokens that are disjoint from calibration (2.1M scored tokens, BF16 KV cache on both sides). Ratios are relative to BF16 on eight GPUs. 75 Beam Model Technical Report, Reflection Team et al. 4.6 Speculative Decoding Decoding large mixture-of-experts model is memory-bound, which leaves most of the GPUs compute idle. Speculative decoding [121, 122] puts this compute to use by having small draft model propose several tokens, which the target model then verifies in single forward pass. With rejection sampling, the targets output distribution is preserved exactly. The speedup depends on the acceptance length 𝜏, the mean number of tokens produced per verification step, and on the cost of drafting. Beam is released with DFlash 2 drafter [123, 124], which increases its decode throughput by 1.9 to 3.0. 4.6.1 Architecture The drafter is 1.93B-parameter block-diffusion model that proposes block of tokens in one forward pass. Its five transformer layers attend bidirectionally within the block and, through their keys and values, to Beams hidden states at layers 4, 16, 28, 40 and 46, the inputs of its global-attention layers. DFlash 2s in-block convolutions and path selector keep drafted tokens consistent, and the embedding and output head are Beams, kept frozen. Context attention is limited to 4,096-token window, so drafting cost stays constant as contexts grow. Whether such local drafter stays accurate deep into long contexts is the main question for training. 4.6.2 Training Data All targets are generated by Beam: the 1.42M PerfectBlend prompts [125], regenerated with the released checkpoint, and rollouts from the multi-teacher on-policy distillation (MOPD) stage that produced Beam (Section 4.3), which cover the agentic and reasoning interactions it is deployed on. After the first 50 steps of that stage, the policys per-token likelihood of its own samples and their lengths were flat in every category, and we use rollouts from these later steps. In ablations with pre-release versions of Beam, replacing 42% of PerfectBlend with such rollouts increased accepted draft tokens by 9.9%, and by 21% on agentic traces. 4.6.3 Training Mostly at Short Context Each time sequence is used, single forward pass of Beam captures its features, and each of its 512 blocks of 16 tokens, starting at randomly sampled anchor positions, reads the features of the tokens before its anchor. Since the cost of this capture, like that of attention, grows with sequence length, we train mostly on short sequences. Beams features shift with position (its global-attention layers scale queries with absolute position [18]), but this does not prevent transfer to long contexts: in development experiments on 43 long agentic traces, drafter trained only at 8K accepted 4.70 draft tokens per block of 16 at 4K to 8K of context and 5.02 beyond 64K. further long-context stage added gains only at longer contexts, 1.6% at 8K to 16K and 3.8% beyond 64K, and these saturated within 4K steps. Since this is small relative to its cost, we keep that stage short: 6 epochs over 2.2M traces truncated to 8K tokens, then 2 epochs over 592K traces of up to 128K tokens. The loss weights each block position by the expected number of accepted tokens that depend on it [126, 127]. To train stably, we lowered AdamWs 𝛽2 to 0.95 and added adaptive gradient clipping [128], which eliminated the gradient spikes that occasionally made early runs diverge despite fixed clipping threshold. Beams features are captured online from its NVFP4 checkpoint, the one we serve, and using BF16 instead changed accepted tokens by at most 1.5%, in training or serving. In total, both stages took about 3.4K B300 GPU-hours. 4.6.4 Sizing for Serving Speed Higher acceptance does not always give higher speed, because drafting and verification have costs. Eight drafter layers instead of five added 2.8% accepted tokens in replay and 1.2% when served, but changed the speedup by only 0.5%, within noise, for 60% more parameters. Block size shows the same trade-off. Verifying 8 positions instead of 16 lowered acceptance length by 5% to 15%, but late positions are rarely accepted and each one still costs verification compute, so serving with 8 positions was faster in 11 of 12 workload and concurrency settings: on chat, the speedup rose from 1.63 to 1.93 for one request and from 1.46 to 2.00 at 128 concurrent requests. Training is not bound by verification cost, so we train with blocks of 16, as DFlash does: drafter trained on larger blocks can be served at smaller ones with little loss, but not the reverse [123]. The released drafter has five layers, trains with blocks of 16 and serves with blocks of 8. 4.6.5 Results With Beam in NVFP4 on four B300 GPUs and 7 drafted tokens per step, the drafter reaches 𝜏 = 4.38 with sampling and 4.64 with greedy decoding, out of maximum of 8, over 1,562 turns of math, code, long-context and chat. Beam Model Technical Report, Reflection Team et al. In line with the transfer result, 𝜏 on DeepSWE agentic traces [129] stays between 4.2 and 4.6 from 16K to 128K tokens of context  (Table 18)  . Decode throughput increases by 1.96 to 3.03 for single request and by 1.89 to 2.75 with 32 concurrent requests  (Table 17)  . sections.title: 5 Evaluations
sections.content: 5.1 Post-Trained Model Evaluations We evaluate Beam across software engineering, mathematics and science, tool use and search, and general capabilities. Section 7 presents the safety evaluations separately. We compare Beam to multiple open-weight models available at the time of announcement on October 16, 2026. The results show the models strengths in coding and agentic tasks. Beam advances the Western open-weight frontier. The model is competitive with larger open models like GLM 5.2 and approaches Qwen 3.8-Max on coding and agentic tasks. Beams advantage lies in its token efficiency at inference time, even though frontier open models like Kimi K3 remain ahead on raw capability. This efficiency was learned through RL: we trained with controllable length penalty that rewarded successful solutions while penalizing unnecessary output tokens beyond per-effort budget. Figure 40 shows the effect on DeepSWE v1.1 evaluations over the course of training: the model first learns to solve the same tasks with fewer tokens, and as agentic capabilities grow, the additional tokens at higher reasoning efforts translate into higher performance. We use published architecture specifications for the Nemotron, GLM, Kimi, Qwen, and DeepSeek models [130 134]. For DeepSeek V4.1 Flash, we report 16B active parameters during decoding (8B during prefill) and total of 748B, comprising the 552B backbone and 196B conditional memory [134]. All evaluations were run using temperature of 0.7, top-𝑝 of 0.99, and reasoning effort 512. 5.1.1 Agentic Coding and Terminal Use We assess software engineering with benchmarks that require repository inspection, code changes, and verification over multiple steps. Table 19 shows the results. DeepSWE uses original engineering tasks [135]; its v1.1 revision grades committed code in clean environment [136]. Terminal-Bench evaluates task completion in commandline environments [62]; the results here use version 2.1 [137]. SWE-Bench Pro evaluates long-horizon software 77 Beam Model Technical Report, Reflection Team et al. Figure 40: Enhanced token efficiency through RL. DeepSWE pass@1 against mean output and tool tokens per episode; each curve is one RL checkpoint (darker is later), each point reasoning effort from 64 to 512. engineering [138, 139]. We separately evaluate on the original 731-task public test split (v1), and on the 51task HARD subset of its revised public release (v2). The HARD subset contains tasks that at least two of five reference model families failed under Scales evaluation protocol, after ambiguous tasks were excluded. SWE Atlas Codebase QnA evaluates code comprehension through technical questions that require running software and reasoning across multiple files [140]. SWE-bench Multilingual evaluates software issue resolution across nine programming languages [141]. SWE-bench Verified evaluates software issue resolution on human-validated subset of SWE-bench [142].
